title: Scientific Foundations - Exam One
description: Exercise Science, Sport Psychology and Nutrition. Section 1 of the exam.

questions.question: A sprinter is doing repeated maximal 5-second efforts. According to the sliding-filament theory, which two substances must be present inside the muscle fiber for crossbridge cycling to keep occurring?
options: Sodium and inorganic phosphate
Calcium and ATP
ADP and iron
questions.explanation: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin to expose actin binding sites, and ATP hydrolysis by myosin ATPase powers the power stroke and crossbridge detachment. Without both, crossbridge cycling stops.

questions.question: You are explaining a motor unit to a new intern. Which description is accurate?
options: A single muscle fiber and all of the motor neurons that innervate it
A motor neuron and all of the muscle fibers it innervates
An upper motor neuron paired with a lower motor neuron
questions.explanation: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates. Because of the all-or-none principle, when the neuron fires, all of those fibers contract together.

questions.question: Two untrained athletes perform the same submaximal arm curl. As the load gets heavier and more force is needed, what is the body's main strategy for increasing the muscle's force output?
options: Partially activating a larger fraction of fibers within each already-active motor unit
Recruiting additional, higher-threshold motor units and increasing firing frequency
Slowing the conduction velocity along the active motor neurons
questions.explanation: Force is graded by recruiting more motor units (size principle, low- then high-threshold) and by increasing firing frequency so twitches summate. Individual fibers within an active unit cannot be partially activated.

questions.question: An endurance runner has a high proportion of Type I fibers in the working muscles. Compared to Type IIx fibers, those Type I fibers would be expected to have:
options: Higher fatigue resistance and higher mitochondrial and capillary density
Higher force production and a faster contraction speed
A higher recruitment threshold and larger fiber diameter
questions.explanation: Type I fibers have more mitochondria, more capillary contacts, more myoglobin, and high fatigue resistance, favoring aerobic metabolism. Type II fibers produce more force, contract faster, and have higher recruitment thresholds.

questions.question: During a heavy biceps curl, the elbow acts as a third-class lever. Because the muscle's moment arm is much shorter than the resistance's moment arm, what does this mean for the biceps?
options: The muscle force needed is much greater than the resistive (external) force
The muscle operates at a mechanical advantage greater than 1.0
The muscle force needed is much less than the external resistance
questions.explanation: In a third-class lever the muscle moment arm is shorter than the resistance moment arm, so mechanical advantage is below 1.0 and the internal muscle force must exceed the external load. This is why internal muscle and tendon forces are so high.

questions.question: A coach wants an athlete to jump 40 cm, which requires a fixed takeoff impulse. The athlete can hit that impulse either with a big force over a short time or a smaller force over a longer time. Which biomechanical relationship explains why the SAME jump height can be reached either way?
options: The force-velocity relationship
The impulse-momentum relationship (force x time = change in momentum)
The Frank-Starling mechanism
questions.explanation: Impulse equals force times time and equals the change in momentum. Since the required change in velocity (and thus impulse) is fixed for a given jump height, the athlete can trade off force against time to achieve it.

questions.question: A lifter performs a barbell overhead press, then lowers it under control. During the lowering (eccentric) phase, how is the work classified?
options: Positive work, because force is still being applied
Zero work, because the muscle is not shortening
Negative work, because the displacement is downward
questions.explanation: Work is force times displacement. During lowering the force stays positive (controlling the bar) but displacement is negative (downward), so the work performed is negative.

questions.question: A pennate muscle and a non-pennate (longitudinal) muscle have the same overall size. Which statement about the pennate muscle is correct?
options: It packs more sarcomeres in parallel, so it generates more force but has a lower maximal shortening velocity
It has more sarcomeres in series, giving it a higher maximal shortening velocity
Its angle of pennation is fixed and cannot change with training
questions.explanation: Greater pennation means more sarcomeres in parallel and fewer in series, which boosts force capability but lowers maximal shortening velocity. Pennation angle also increases as the muscle shortens and is modifiable with training.

questions.question: An athlete does a maximal 6-second effort, like a short sprint or a single heavy set. Which energy system is the primary supplier of ATP for that effort?
options: The oxidative (aerobic) system
Fast glycolysis
The phosphagen system
questions.explanation: For extremely high-intensity efforts of about 0 to 6 seconds, the phosphagen system (ATP stores plus the creatine kinase reaction with creatine phosphate) is the primary energy source because it produces ATP at the highest rate.

questions.question: An athlete reports a burning sensation during high-intensity exercise and blames lactic acid. Based on current bioenergetics, what is the most accurate correction?
options: Lactate is not the cause of fatigue; proton (H+) accumulation, largely from ATP hydrolysis, drives the drop in pH (metabolic acidosis)
Lactic acid dissociates immediately and is the direct cause of the acidosis and fatigue
Lactate accumulation accelerates metabolic acidosis by adding protons to the cell
questions.explanation: The lactate dehydrogenase reaction actually consumes a proton; the term is metabolic acidosis, not lactic acidosis. The H+ accumulation comes mainly from ATP hydrolysis, and lactate is itself used as a fuel and even helps buffer acidosis.

questions.question: When glycolysis starts from a molecule of MUSCLE GLYCOGEN rather than blood glucose, why is the net ATP yield from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis higher (3 vs 2)?
options: Glycogen produces an extra pyruvate molecule
Glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated, so it bypasses the first ATP-consuming step
Glycogen breakdown directly produces an extra ATP in the electron transport chain
questions.explanation: Blood glucose must be phosphorylated on entry (costing 1 ATP), but glucose freed from glycogen by glycogen phosphorylase is already phosphorylated. So glycogen uses only 1 ATP and nets 3, while blood glucose uses 2 and nets 2.

questions.question: A coach is programming interval work to develop the phosphagen system using roughly 5-10 second high-power efforts. Which work-to-rest ratio range best fits that goal?
questions.explanation: Phosphagen-focused intervals (about 90-100% of max power, 5-10 s of work) use long rest, roughly 1:12 to 1:20, because full creatine phosphate resynthesis is aerobic and can take 3-5 minutes (up to 8). Shorter rest ratios target glycolytic or oxidative systems.

questions.question: A strength coach wants to maximize the acute anabolic hormone response of a workout. Which design pattern is most consistently linked to the largest acute increases in serum testosterone and the 22 kD GH isoform?
options: Large muscle-group, high-volume work with short rest periods
Single-joint isolation moves with very long (5+ min) rest periods
Low-volume, low-intensity work that avoids glycolytic stress
questions.explanation: The acute hormonal response tracks the total work and metabolic demand. Protocols using large muscle groups, high volume, and short rest drive the glycolytic system and H+ production, which is associated with the largest acute testosterone, GH, and cortisol responses.

questions.question: Hormones such as testosterone and cortisol are carried in the blood by binding proteins (e.g., sex hormone-binding globulin, albumin). What is the primary functional role these binding proteins play?
options: They permanently block the hormone from ever reaching a receptor
They serve as temporary storage and protect the hormone from degradation, extending its half-life
They convert steroid hormones into peptide hormones for faster signaling
questions.explanation: Binding proteins act as a temporary reservoir and shield hormones from breakdown, lengthening their half-life and regulating how much free, bioactive hormone is available to tissues.

questions.question: An athlete chronically overtrains with very high-volume heavy resistance work and poor recovery, leading to downregulation of beta-2 receptors. What does this specifically impair?
options: Insulin's ability to clear blood glucose, causing hyperglycemia
Thyroid hormone's permissive effect on metabolic rate
The interaction with epinephrine, reducing muscle contractile force
questions.explanation: When a hormone stays chronically elevated, receptors can desensitize or downregulate. Heavy resistance overtraining can downregulate beta-2 receptors, blunting their response to epinephrine and reducing the catecholamine-driven contractile force.

questions.question: Cortisol is labeled a 'catabolic' hormone, yet acute increases after a hard session are not purely harmful. What beneficial acute role does cortisol play in muscle remodeling?
options: It directly stimulates actin and myosin synthesis
It helps clear damaged proteins and helps maintain blood glucose
It upregulates androgen receptor content for 48-72 hours
questions.explanation: Although chronically high cortisol is detrimental and catabolic, acute post-exercise increases contribute to tissue remodeling by helping clear damaged proteins and maintaining blood glucose during the stress of training.

questions.question: In untrained people the ability to maximally recruit motor units is limited. Where does the increased motor unit activation that drives early strength gains primarily originate?
options: At the neuromuscular junction with increased acetylcholine release
In the higher brain centers (motor cortex) with the intent to produce maximal force
In the Golgi tendon organs through reduced inhibition only
questions.explanation: Increased motor unit activation begins in the higher brain centers: the intent to produce maximal force raises primary motor cortex activity, with adaptations then reflected down the descending corticospinal tracts and improved recruitment of high-threshold motor units.

questions.question: As a muscle hypertrophies with resistance (anaerobic) training, what happens to its mitochondrial density and capillary density?
options: Both increase in proportion to the fiber size gain
Mitochondrial density increases while capillary density stays exactly constant
Both tend to decrease (no change or decrease), because fiber CSA grows disproportionately to them
questions.explanation: Density is expressed relative to muscle area. Because cross-sectional area grows faster than mitochondria or capillaries proliferate, both mitochondrial density and capillary density show no change or a decrease with heavy resistance training hypertrophy.

questions.question: A coach is told that resistance training shifts muscle fiber type. Which transition along the fiber-type continuum does heavy resistance/anaerobic training typically produce?
options: Type IIx shifting toward Type IIa (more fatigue-resistant)
Type IIa shifting toward Type IIx (more glycolytic)
Type I shifting toward Type IIx (more powerful)
questions.explanation: Consistent activation moves fibers along the continuum from IIx toward the intermediate IIax and then to IIa. This positive shift reflects greater fatigue resistance at similar absolute force output, along with hypertrophy.

questions.question: Two weeks (14 days) after a competitive weightlifter stops training entirely, what does the detraining research describe as the earliest muscular change?
options: An immediate, large decline in slow-twitch (Type I) fiber cross-sectional area
A measurable decline specifically in fast-twitch fiber cross-sectional area, with slow-twitch initially unchanged
A complete reversal of fiber type distribution back to untrained values
questions.explanation: In strength/sprint athletes, fast-twitch fiber CSA declines rapidly; one study found about a 6.4% drop in fast-twitch CSA in 14 days, while slow-twitch fibers showed no significant immediate change. Fiber-type distribution itself was unaffected at 14 days.

questions.question: The single most significant cardiovascular adaptation to long-term aerobic endurance training is an increase in maximal cardiac output. What primarily drives that increase?
options: A large increase in maximal heart rate
An increase in resting heart rate
An increase in stroke volume (via larger left ventricle and greater contractility)
questions.explanation: Maximal heart rate stays unchanged or even decreases slightly with training, so the rise in maximal cardiac output comes from improved stroke volume, driven by a larger left ventricle (chamber volume and wall thickness) and stronger contractions.

questions.question: A well-trained endurance runner can sustain a high percentage of VO2max before blood lactate accumulates. In a trained athlete, the onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA) occurs at roughly what percentage of aerobic capacity?
options: About 40%-50% of aerobic capacity
About 60%-65% of aerobic capacity
Up to about 80%-90% of aerobic capacity
questions.explanation: Aerobic training raises the lactate threshold so that lactate production matches clearance up to a higher relative intensity. In trained athletes OBLA can occur at up to 80%-90% of aerobic capacity, allowing harder sustained efforts.

questions.question: Two distance runners have identical VO2max and lactate threshold values, yet one consistently races faster. This difference is best attributed to which factor?
options: Better exercise economy
A higher maximal heart rate
A larger arteriovenous oxygen difference at rest
questions.explanation: Exercise economy, largely a function of biomechanics and technique plus metabolic, cardiovascular, and neuromuscular efficiency, lets one athlete hold a higher pace for the same energy cost even when VO2max and lactate threshold are equal.

questions.question: An endurance coach is comparing altitude training and heat acclimation. What is the principal physiological adaptation each one targets?
options: Both primarily increase maximal heart rate
Altitude increases hemoglobin/red cell volume (via EPO); heat acclimation expands plasma volume
Altitude expands plasma volume; heat acclimation primarily raises VO2max by reducing core temperature
questions.explanation: Altitude raises EPO, increasing hemoglobin mass and red cell volume to boost oxygen-carrying capacity, while heat acclimation produces a large expansion of plasma volume that raises stroke volume. They improve aerobic performance through different mechanisms.

questions.question: A youth coach is told muscle mass increases substantially during puberty in boys. This pubertal increase in muscle mass is due primarily to what?
options: Hyperplasia (an increase in the number of muscle fibers)
A decrease in body fat being reclassified as muscle
Hypertrophy of individual muscle fibers driven by rising hormones
questions.explanation: In both sexes the pubertal increase in muscle mass comes from hypertrophy of individual fibers, not hyperplasia. In boys, rising testosterone, GH, and IGF drive a marked gain in muscle mass.

questions.question: A preadolescent boy completes a well-designed resistance program and gets noticeably stronger but shows little muscle size change. What best explains the strength gains in young children?
options: Large hypertrophy driven by high circulating testosterone
Neuromuscular (motor development) adaptations, since circulating anabolic hormones are low before puberty
Hyperplasia stimulated by the resistance stimulus
questions.explanation: Preadolescents have low circulating testosterone, GH, and IGF, so they struggle to add muscle mass. Their strength gains come predominantly from neuromuscular adaptations and motor development rather than hypertrophy.

questions.question: An S&C professional designing resistance training for older adults (over 65) should generally do which of the following for safety?
options: Encourage the Valsalva maneuver to maximize trunk stiffness
Avoid all aerobic work and train the same muscles daily
Discourage the Valsalva maneuver and allow 48 to 72 hours of recovery between sessions
questions.explanation: The Valsalva maneuver is generally discouraged in seniors because of the sharp rise in blood pressure, especially with cardiovascular contraindications. Recommendations include 48-72 hours of recovery between sessions and concurrent aerobic, resistance, and balance work.

questions.question: Female athletes have a higher rate of noncontact ACL injuries. What is believed to be the single most significant contributing factor?
options: A neuromuscular deficiency leading to abnormal biomechanics such as increased dynamic knee valgus
A smaller femoral notch size alone
Greater absolute upper-body strength
questions.explanation: While anatomical factors (femoral notch size, tibial slope, ligament laxity) contribute, the text identifies neuromuscular deficiency as the most significant factor, producing abnormal biomechanics like increased dynamic knee valgus on landing. This makes neuromuscular/plyometric training key for prevention.

questions.question: When comparing strength between the sexes, the gap shrinks dramatically under one condition. Which statement reflects this?
options: Females are stronger than males in absolute upper-body strength
When strength is normalized to muscle volume (relative basis), sex differences are greatly reduced
Absolute upper-body strength of females is closer to male values than lower-body strength is
questions.explanation: Females have a similar number of muscle fibers as males, and when strength is expressed relative to muscle volume the values are similar. Absolute differences (driven by larger fiber size in males) are largest in the upper body; lower-body absolute strength is closer to male values.

questions.question: A female endurance athlete shows greater fatigue resistance in long events despite a lower VO2max relative to body size than her male counterparts. Which sex difference best explains this fatigue resistance?
options: A greater proportion of Type I oxidative fibers and higher fat oxidation
A higher absolute testosterone concentration driving more hypertrophy
A greater reliance on carbohydrate and protein during prolonged exercise
questions.explanation: Females tend to have a greater proportion of Type I oxidative fibers and higher mitochondrial respiration, so they oxidize more fat and less carbohydrate/protein during prolonged work, supporting greater fatigue resistance even with a lower relative VO2max.

questions.question: An athlete is described as having a general physiological and psychological activation that varies on a continuum from deep sleep to intense excitement. Which construct does this describe?
options: State anxiety
Arousal
Trait anxiety
questions.explanation: Arousal is simply a blend of physiological and psychological activation that ranges from comatose to highly excited, and by itself is neither pleasant nor unpleasant. Anxiety is a negatively perceived subcategory of arousal.

questions.question: A lifter shows up to a meet with a fast heart rate, an upset stomach, and visibly tense muscles. These physical symptoms are best classified as which component of anxiety?
options: Cognitive anxiety
Trait anxiety
Somatic anxiety
questions.explanation: Somatic anxiety is the physical reaction component, shown through symptoms like tachycardia, upset stomach, and muscle tension. Cognitive anxiety is the mental piece (worry, negative thoughts).

questions.question: A coach insists that the more psyched up an athlete gets, the better they will perform, in a straight linear fashion. Which theory is the coach relying on, and what is its main limitation?
options: Inverted-U theory; it ignores cognitive anxiety
Drive theory; performers can be too pumped up to perform well
Catastrophe theory; it predicts only gradual declines
questions.explanation: Hull's drive theory proposes arousal and performance rise together linearly, but this breaks down because performers can clearly be too aroused to perform, especially on complex or poorly learned skills.

questions.question: How does the individual zones of optimal functioning (IZOF) theory differ from the basic inverted-U hypothesis?
options: Optimal performance always occurs at the midpoint of the arousal continuum
Best performance occurs within a small range of arousal that varies by individual, not at a single fixed midpoint
Only somatic arousal matters; cognitive anxiety is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Hanin's IZOF holds that ideal performance does not always sit at the midpoint and that each athlete has an individual bandwidth of optimal arousal, rather than one universal optimal point.

questions.question: According to catastrophe theory, what happens when high physiological arousal occurs together with high cognitive anxiety?
options: A gradual, proportionate decline in performance
A sudden, sharp drop in performance rather than a gradual decline
An immediate boost in performance from the combined activation
questions.explanation: Catastrophe theory says that under high cognitive anxiety, once arousal passes a point, performance can drop catastrophically and suddenly, and simply restoring calm does not automatically return prior performance levels.

questions.question: Two athletes feel the exact same level of pre-game arousal. One reads it as excitement and anticipation; the other reads it as scary and worrisome. Which theory best explains why the same arousal helps one and hurts the other?
options: Drive theory
Inverted-U theory
Reversal theory
questions.explanation: Kerr's reversal theory emphasizes that it is the individual's interpretation of arousal, not just the amount, that determines whether it helps or hurts, and athletes can choose to reverse that interpretation.

questions.question: An athlete who is dominated by the motive to achieve success (MAS) is most drawn to which kind of challenge?
options: Tasks that are nearly impossible, so failure carries no shame
Tasks that are very easy, guaranteeing success
Uncertain or challenging tasks with roughly a 50% probability of success
questions.explanation: MAS-dominated athletes seek challenging or uncertain situations (about 50% chance of success) because these best let them test and take pride in their abilities. MAF-dominated athletes prefer very easy or very hard tasks to avoid shame.

questions.question: A strength coach wants to boost a young lifter's intrinsic motivation. Based on self-determination, which approach fits best?
options: Give the athlete some latitude in decision making and set process goals that build perceived competence
Rely heavily on cash bonuses for every personal record
Remove all athlete input and issue strict authoritarian directives at all times
questions.explanation: Deci's view ties intrinsic motivation to competence and self-determination, so allowing decision-making latitude raises perceived self-determination and appropriate process goals raise perceived competence; a total lack of delegated responsibility can kill drive.

questions.question: Bandura lists several sources of self-efficacy. Which one consists of past experiences of success or failure, and is considered especially influential?
options: Verbal persuasion
Performance accomplishments
Vicarious experiences
questions.explanation: Per Bandura, performance accomplishments (past experiences of success or failure) are one of the key sources of self-efficacy; others include vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, imaginal experiences, and physiological and emotional states.

questions.question: A coach tells a wrestler trying to cut weight to focus on the daily actions he controls, such as completing his aerobic work and hitting his dietary plan, rather than on the number on the scale at weigh-in. What type of goal is the coach emphasizing?
options: Outcome goal
Process goal
Subjective goal
questions.explanation: Process goals focus on the controllable actions an athlete performs to execute the skill well, so success is strongly tied to effort. Outcome goals (like the final weight or winning) depend partly on factors outside the athlete's control.

questions.question: A coach notices a high school athlete who, over the past six weeks, has a worsening mood, is missing practices and school, has stopped self-care, and reports no longer caring about the sport. Following the textbook's three-step approach, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Treat it as a normal subclinical dip and wait a few days for it to pass
Refer the athlete to a qualified mental health professional such as a counselor or psychologist
Increase the athlete's training load to rebuild motivation
questions.explanation: Persistent distress (greater than 2-3 weeks) that disrupts sleep, self-care, and social or academic functioning warrants referral to a qualified mental health professional, not self-reflection alone or training changes.

questions.question: Which feature most distinguishes depression from anxiety, given that the two share signs like agitation, somatic complaints, and rumination?
options: Worry and circular thinking
Rapid heart rate and sweating
Anhedonia, hopelessness or helplessness, and low energy
questions.explanation: Depression and anxiety overlap on agitation, somatic complaints, and rumination, but what sets depression apart is anhedonia (lack of emotion), feelings of hopelessness or helplessness, and low energy.

questions.question: An athlete on your team has been diagnosed with diabetes and needs help managing his diet around his medication and training. As the strength and conditioning professional, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Build the meal plan yourself, since you already act as his sports nutrition coach
Refer him to a sports dietitian (registered dietitian), since this requires medical nutrition therapy
Tell him to just follow MyPlate, since it is the standard guideline for everyone
questions.explanation: More complex situations in which food or nutrition is used to treat or manage a medical condition (such as diabetes or a nutrient deficiency) require medical nutrition therapy, which falls under the role of the sports dietitian (a registered dietitian). An S&C professional can act as a sports nutrition coach for basic education only.

questions.question: A 90 kg strength athlete wants to build muscle mass. Using the textbook's recommended protein range for strength athletes, which daily protein intake falls within the appropriate target?
options: About 270 g/day (3.0 g/kg)
About 72 g/day (0.8 g/kg)
About 150 g/day (1.7 g/kg)
questions.explanation: Strength athletes should consume 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day. At 90 kg that is roughly 126-180 g/day, so 150 g (1.7 g/kg) fits. The 0.8 g/kg figure is the RDA for the general adult population, not athletes.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a low-glycemic-index food and how an athlete might use it?
options: Low-GI foods are digested and absorbed slowly, causing a smaller rise in blood glucose; athletes can base their everyday choices on them while saving high-GI foods for around training
Low-GI foods spike blood glucose rapidly, making them the best choice immediately before competition
Low-GI foods contain no carbohydrate, so they have no effect on insulin release
questions.explanation: Low-GI foods (vegetables, legumes, whole grains) are digested slowly, producing a smaller rise in blood glucose and insulin. Athletes can use low-GI foods as the base of their diet for health while reserving high-GI foods in and around exercise for rapid energy and glycogen replenishment.

questions.question: An aerobic endurance athlete is in her most demanding training phase. Roughly how much carbohydrate should she aim to consume to support that training?
options: 0.8 to 1.0 g/kg body weight per day
8 to 10 g/kg body weight per day
20 to 25 g/kg body weight per day
questions.explanation: Aerobic endurance athletes should aim for 8 to 10 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight per day during their most demanding training phases or competition, alongside 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day of protein. The other ranges are far too low or implausibly high.

questions.question: A marathoner finishes a glycogen-depleting race and has another hard session in under 12 hours. To replenish glycogen, what is the recommended approach for carbohydrate intake immediately after exercise?
options: Consume about 1.0 to 1.85 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight per hour, starting right after exercise and at regular intervals for up to 5 hours
Avoid carbohydrate for at least 5 hours so the muscle can recover before refueling
Consume only protein, since carbohydrate timing has no effect on glycogen resynthesis
questions.explanation: For rapid glycogen replenishment, athletes should consume roughly 1.0 to 1.85 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight per hour immediately after exercise and at regular intervals (every 15-60 min) for up to 5 hours. This matters most when recovery time before the next bout is short.

questions.question: A 68 kg distance cyclist plans to carbohydrate load before a long road race. Which scenario best reflects a use of carbohydrate loading consistent with the textbook?
options: He loads carbohydrate before a 30-minute sprint workout to maximize power output
He follows several days of high carbohydrate intake (e.g., 8-12 g/kg/day) with tapered training before an event lasting more than 90 minutes
He cuts carbohydrate to near zero the day before to force his body to burn fat during the race
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate loading uses high carbohydrate intake (commonly 8-12 g/kg/day) in the days before competition, paired with tapering, to maximize muscle glycogen. It benefits athletes training or competing for more than 90 minutes, such as distance cyclists and runners, not short high-power efforts.

questions.question: A 70 kg athlete wants to use creatine monohydrate and asks about a body-weight-based loading and maintenance protocol. Which dosing scheme matches the textbook recommendation?
options: Load with 0.3 g/kg/day for about 5 days, then maintain with 0.03 g/kg/day
Load with 3.0 g/kg/day for about 5 days, then maintain with 0.3 g/kg/day
Load with 0.03 g/kg/day for about 5 days, then maintain with 0.3 g/kg/day
questions.explanation: A typical creatine regimen is a loading dose of about 20-25 g/day (or 0.3 g/kg body mass) for 5 days, followed by a maintenance dose of about 2 g/day (or 0.03 g/kg body mass per day). Creatine reliably increases maximal strength, power, and lean body mass.

questions.question: An endurance athlete asks about erythropoietin (EPO) as a way to boost performance. What is the major health risk that makes EPO dangerous for athletes?
options: It lowers red blood cell count, causing anemia and reduced oxygen delivery
It has no meaningful physiological effect and is banned purely on ethical grounds
It increases hematocrit and blood viscosity, raising the risk of clotting, elevated blood pressure, stroke, and embolism
questions.explanation: EPO increases red blood cell mass, which raises hematocrit and blood viscosity (thicker blood). This increases the risk of clotting, elevated systolic blood pressure, stroke, and cerebral or pulmonary embolism, and deaths of competitive cyclists have been linked to EPO use.

title: Scientific Foundations - Exam Two
description: Exercise Science, Sport Psychology and Nutrition. Section 1 of the exam.

questions.question: Two athletes have biceps of identical fiber type and pennation, but one has a larger physiological cross-sectional area. A coach wants to explain, in sliding-filament terms, the single most direct determinant of the force either muscle can express at a given instant. Which statement is correct?
options: The instantaneous number of attached actin-myosin cross-bridges, which the larger cross-section can support in greater number
The tensile stiffness of the epimysium and surrounding connective tissue that transmits the pull to the tendon
The concentration of stored sarcoplasmic glycogen available to fuel the contraction
questions.explanation: Force production is dictated by the number of actin and myosin cross-bridges attached at a given moment. A larger physiological cross-sectional area holds more parallel contractile filaments, so more potential cross-bridges and greater force. Connective tissue and stored glycogen do not set the instantaneous force ceiling.

questions.question: An intern watches an athlete grind out a maximal lift and concludes that the nervous system must be sending a 'stronger' signal that makes each recruited motor unit's fibers contract harder. Applying the all-or-none principle, how should you correct this?
options: A stronger central drive selectively activates a fraction of a unit's fibers with more force, sparing the rest
Once a motor unit fires, all its fibers contract together and one action potential cannot grade that twitch; whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more units and by rate coding
The action potential itself can be amplified so that a single motor unit twitch produces more force
questions.explanation: By the all-or-none principle, every fiber in a motor unit contracts fully or not at all, and a single action potential cannot partially activate the unit or vary one twitch's force. Whole-muscle force is graded instead by recruiting additional motor units and by increasing firing rate (rate coding).

questions.question: A coach describes two receptors: receptor A lies parallel to the working fibers and fires when the muscle is stretched quickly, while receptor B lies in series with the fibers and fires as the muscle-tendon unit builds tension. Which pairing correctly names A and B and what each primarily senses?
options: Both A and B are tension sensors; they differ only in how fast they respond
A is the Golgi tendon organ sensing tension; B is the muscle spindle sensing length and rate of stretch
A is the muscle spindle sensing muscle length and rate of stretch; B is the Golgi tendon organ sensing muscle-tendon tension
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles lie parallel to extrafusal fibers and sense muscle length and the rate of length change, triggering the stretch reflex. Golgi tendon organs sit in series within the tendon and respond to muscle tension, reflexively inhibiting the agonist when tension is high. The parallel/quick-stretch receptor is the spindle; the in-series/tension receptor is the GTO.

questions.question: Mid-rep on a maximal back squat the load exceeds what the athlete can control, and a reflex acts to reduce agonist tension to protect the muscle-tendon unit. Which receptor drives this protective inhibition, and where does it sit?
options: The Golgi tendon organ, positioned in series near the myotendinous junction
The muscle spindle, which reflexively raises agonist activation via the stretch reflex
The Pacinian corpuscle in the joint capsule, signaling deep pressure
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs sit in series near the myotendinous junction and respond to high tension by reflexively inhibiting the agonist, a protective response. Muscle spindles do the opposite, exciting the agonist via the stretch reflex; Pacinian corpuscles detect pressure/vibration and do not provide this protective inhibition.

questions.question: A triceps pushdown is modeled as a lever in which the triceps inserts about 5 cm from the elbow axis while the resistance acts about 40 cm from that axis. Working from the moment arms, what does this arrangement require of the muscle?
options: It gives a mechanical advantage above 1.0, so the muscle can use less force than the external resistance
It gives a mechanical advantage of about 0.125, so the muscle must generate force roughly eight times the resistance
It gives a mechanical advantage of about 1.0, so muscle force equals the resistance
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage equals the muscle (force) moment arm divided by the resistance moment arm, here 5/40 = 0.125. Being well below 1.0, the muscle must generate force about eight times larger than the external resistance to balance the torques.

questions.question: A weightlifter and a bodybuilder have similar muscle volume, but the bodybuilder's biceps has a markedly greater pennation angle. Compared with the more longitudinally arranged muscle, what is the most likely functional consequence of that higher pennation angle?
options: A higher maximal shortening velocity measured along the muscle's line of pull
Fewer total contractile fibers in the muscle and therefore lower maximal force output
More fibers packed into a given cross-section, favoring force production at the expense of shortening velocity along the line of pull
questions.explanation: A pennate arrangement packs more fibers into a given cross-sectional area, raising force potential, but because the fibers pull at an oblique angle to the tendon, shortening velocity along the line of pull is reduced. So higher pennation trades velocity for force, not the reverse.

questions.question: Two athletes have geometrically similar builds, but one is considerably smaller and lighter. In tasks like sprinting and vertical jumping that require moving one's own body, which athlete tends to have the edge, and why?
options: The smaller athlete, because with similar proportions body mass grows faster than strength, yielding a higher strength-to-mass ratio
The larger athlete, because muscular strength scales in direct proportion to body mass, preserving performance
Neither, because in geometrically similar athletes the strength-to-mass ratio is constant across body sizes
questions.explanation: As body size increases with constant proportions, body mass (a volume, roughly length cubed) rises faster than muscular strength (tied to cross-sectional area, roughly length squared). The smaller athlete therefore has the higher strength-to-mass ratio, which directly reflects the ability to accelerate one's own body.

questions.question: A shot-putter explodes through a single all-out throw that lasts roughly 4 seconds. Which energy system supplies the majority of the ATP for that effort, and why is it the primary contributor here?
options: The oxidative system, because it produces the most ATP per substrate molecule
The phosphagen system, because it supplies ATP at the highest rate for very brief maximal efforts
Fast glycolysis, because it dominates from the first second of any high-intensity work
questions.explanation: Very short maximal efforts of roughly 0 to 6 seconds rely primarily on the phosphagen system (stored ATP and creatine phosphate), which supplies ATP at the highest rate but for the shortest duration. The oxidative system is high-yield but slow, and fast glycolysis becomes dominant only as the effort extends beyond a few seconds.

questions.question: During a heavy lift an athlete slowly lowers the bar (lengthening under load), presses it back up (shortening), and then holds it motionless. Ranking these three actions for a given muscle, during which one can the muscle develop the greatest force?
options: The concentric (shortening) action, because active shortening recruits the most cross-bridges
The isometric (static) hold, because zero velocity maximizes cross-bridge attachment time
The eccentric (lengthening) action, which along the force-velocity relationship allows the greatest force
questions.explanation: Along the force-velocity relationship a muscle produces its greatest force during an eccentric (lengthening) action, more than during an isometric hold, and least during a concentric (shortening) action. This is why an athlete can lower more weight than they can lift.

questions.question: A coach programs 5- to 10-second maximal sprints to tax the phosphagen system and asks how long rest should allow for near-complete creatine phosphate recovery. After a maximal effort that heavily depletes creatine phosphate, roughly how long does full CP resynthesis take?
options: About 8 minutes, with roughly half restored in the first 30 seconds or so
About 24 hours, similar to the time course for muscle glycogen repletion
About 30 seconds, at which point creatine phosphate is essentially fully restored
questions.explanation: Full ATP resynthesis takes about 3 to 5 minutes, but full creatine phosphate resynthesis can take up to about 8 minutes, with roughly half restored in the first 30 seconds. The 30-second mark reflects only partial recovery, and 24 hours describes glycogen, not CP.

questions.question: A well-trained distance runner can hold a high fraction of her aerobic capacity before blood lactate climbs sharply. In aerobically trained athletes, the onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA) typically occurs at approximately what percentage of VO2max, and how does that compare with an untrained person?
options: Around 30% to 40% of VO2max, lower than the untrained value because trained athletes accumulate lactate sooner
Around 70% to 80% of VO2max, pushed higher than the roughly 50% to 60% seen in untrained people
Around 50% to 60% of VO2max, essentially the same threshold seen in untrained people
questions.explanation: The lactate threshold begins around 50% to 60% of VO2max in untrained people but is pushed out to roughly 70% to 80% of VO2max in aerobically trained athletes, letting them sustain a higher intensity before lactate accumulates. Training raises, not lowers, this percentage.

questions.question: A triathlete finishes a glycogen-depleting race and must train hard again in under 12 hours, so maximizing muscle glycogen resynthesis is the priority. Which carbohydrate feeding strategy best matches the recommendation for rapid repletion?
options: Withhold carbohydrate until the next full meal so the muscle can rest before refueling
Provide about 0.1 gram of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight once for the day
Provide about 0.7 to 3.0 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight every 2 hours after exercise
questions.explanation: Glycogen repletion is optimized when about 0.7 to 3.0 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight are ingested every 2 hours after exercise, which matters most when a hard session follows soon after. Delaying intake or feeding a trivial dose blunts resynthesis.

questions.question: A strength coach wants a single session designed to produce the largest acute rise in serum testosterone. Which set of program variables best fits that objective?
options: Large-muscle-group, multijoint exercises at heavy loads (about 85% to 95% of 1RM) with moderate-to-high volume and short rest intervals
Single-joint isolation exercises at light loads with very long rest periods between sets
Low-intensity steady-state aerobic work sustained for about 60 minutes
questions.explanation: Acute testosterone elevations are most associated with large-muscle-group, multijoint exercises performed with heavy loads (about 85% to 95% of 1RM), moderate-to-high volume, and short rest intervals. Isolation work with long rests or prolonged low-intensity aerobic exercise does not maximize this acute response.

questions.question: A coach notices an athlete can generate the most force at a mid-range joint angle rather than at full stretch or full shortening. Which mechanism best explains why maximal force capability occurs near the muscle's resting length?
options: At resting length the actin and myosin overlap so little that only a few cross-bridges can form, minimizing internal drag
At resting length the actin-myosin overlap is optimal, allowing the greatest number of cross-bridges to form
Force capability actually peaks when the muscle is maximally shortened, and mid-range is only a testing artifact
questions.explanation: The length-tension relationship shows force capability is greatest near resting length because that length provides optimal actin-myosin overlap and thus the most cross-bridge formation. Force falls off when the muscle is overly shortened (filaments overlap excessively) or overly stretched (too little overlap).

questions.question: Under prolonged stress, cortisol behaves as a catabolic and anti-anabolic hormone in skeletal muscle. Which description captures its primary catabolic action?
options: It drives protein synthesis and promotes glycogen storage within the muscle
It stimulates erythropoiesis, increasing red blood cell production in the bone marrow
It promotes protein breakdown and shunts amino acids toward glucose formation while suppressing protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Cortisol exerts catabolic and anti-anabolic effects: it promotes protein breakdown, directs amino acids toward gluconeogenesis, and inhibits the incorporation of amino acids into protein. Stimulating synthesis or driving red blood cell production are not among its catabolic actions.

questions.question: An untrained athlete gains strength rapidly in the first few weeks of lifting with little measurable change in muscle size, implicating neural adaptation. Assuming a normal recruitment pattern, in what order are that athlete's motor units brought into play as force demand rises?
options: In order of increasing size and threshold, so lower-threshold units are recruited before higher-threshold ones (Henneman's size principle)
In a random order, though in beginners the largest, highest-threshold units tend to fire first
All of the muscle's motor units at once, following the all-or-none principle applied to the whole muscle
questions.explanation: Early strength gains are largely neural, and motor units are normally recruited in order of increasing size and threshold per Henneman's size principle, with smaller, lower-threshold units activated first. Recruitment is orderly, not random, and the all-or-none principle applies to a single motor unit, not the whole muscle at once.

questions.question: At the start of a hard run, oxygen uptake rises slowly and cannot immediately meet the energy demand, so anaerobic sources fill the gap until VO2 catches up. What is the correct term for this early shortfall between the oxygen required and the oxygen actually consumed?
options: Excess postexercise oxygen consumption, reflecting elevated oxygen use after the effort ends
The oxygen deficit, reflecting the early lag before aerobic supply matches demand
The lactate threshold, the intensity at which blood lactate begins to accumulate
questions.explanation: At exercise onset the aerobic system responds slowly, so anaerobic mechanisms supply much of the early energy; the gap between oxygen required and oxygen consumed during this lag is the oxygen deficit. Elevated oxygen use during recovery is EPOC, and the lactate threshold is an intensity marker, not this early shortfall.

questions.question: An athlete asks whether resistance training can increase the actual number of muscle fibers rather than just their size. Based on what has been directly demonstrated in humans, what is the most accurate answer?
options: Yes; hyperplasia through longitudinal fiber splitting is the principal growth mechanism in trained humans
Neither hypertrophy nor hyperplasia has been shown to occur in humans
Only hypertrophy has been directly confirmed in humans; hyperplasia has been shown in some animal models but not confirmed in humans
questions.explanation: Hyperplasia (an increase in fiber number via longitudinal splitting) has been demonstrated in some animal models but not directly confirmed in humans. Hypertrophy, the enlargement of existing fibers, is the established mechanism of resistance-training growth in humans.

questions.question: A coach wants lower-body loading heavy enough to trigger new bone formation. Under the minimal essential strain (MES) concept, the imposed force must exceed roughly what fraction of the bone's fracture force to stimulate osteoblasts?
options: About one-tenth of the force required to fracture the bone
About one-fifth of the force required to fracture the bone
About one-half of the force required to fracture the bone
questions.explanation: The minimal essential strain is thought to be approximately one-tenth (1/10) of the force required to fracture the bone; loads at or above that threshold stimulate osteoblasts to lay down new bone. One-fifth or one-half overstate the threshold.

questions.question: A coach wants resistance training that produces the greatest net growth of tendon and ligament tissue. Which loading approach best achieves that, and why do lighter approaches fall short?
options: Low- to moderate-intensity exercise, because that intensity markedly raises collagen content in connective tissue
High-intensity loading applied through the full range of motion of the joint
Prolonged low-force aerobic exercise such as easy jogging, because sustained loading time drives collagen turnover
questions.explanation: Low- to moderate-intensity exercise does not markedly change collagen content, and low-force endurance work does not drive net connective tissue growth. It is high-intensity loading applied through the full joint range of motion that stimulates net growth of tendons and ligaments.

questions.question: After several months of aerobic training, testing shows the athlete's tissues remove more oxygen from each unit of blood that reaches the working muscles. Which specific adaptation does this reflect, and how does it feed into VO2max?
options: A decreased maximal stroke volume, lowering delivery so extraction appears higher
A reduced muscle capillary density, concentrating oxygen extraction into fewer vessels
An increased arteriovenous oxygen (a-vO2) difference, reflecting greater oxygen extraction that, with higher cardiac output, raises VO2max
questions.explanation: Aerobic training widens the arteriovenous oxygen (a-vO2) difference, meaning tissues extract more oxygen from the blood. Combined with greater maximal cardiac output, this contributes to a higher VO2max. Stroke volume and capillary density actually increase with training, not decrease.

questions.question: After a year of aerobic endurance training a distance runner's maximal cardiac output rises substantially. Given how maximal heart rate behaves with training, which change is chiefly responsible for the higher maximal cardiac output?
options: A rise in maximal stroke volume, while maximal heart rate stays essentially unchanged or drifts slightly lower
A simultaneous fall in both maximal heart rate and maximal stroke volume
A sharp rise in maximal heart rate, while maximal stroke volume stays essentially unchanged
questions.explanation: The most significant cardiovascular adaptation to long-term aerobic training is an increased maximal cardiac output, driven primarily by a higher maximal stroke volume. Maximal heart rate generally remains unaltered or may even decrease slightly, so it is not the driver of the rise.

questions.question: A strength-trained athlete takes an unplanned two-week layoff and worries that fiber-type characteristics will shift. Based on the reported effects of about 14 days of inactivity in strength athletes, what should you tell him?
options: Expect a complete reversal of his strength gains within those 14 days
Expect no significant change in muscle fiber type distribution over 14 days, with minimal loss of maximal strength
Expect a rapid conversion of his Type II fibers to Type I within 14 days
questions.explanation: In strength-trained athletes, about 14 days of inactivity has been reported to have no effect on muscle fiber type distribution, and short layoffs have minimal effect on maximal strength. Neither a full loss of strength nor a fast Type II to Type I conversion occurs over that span.

questions.question: An exercise physiologist explains why aging adults lose muscle power faster than they lose low-intensity endurance. Age-related muscle atrophy is attributed largely to inactivity plus a gradual, selective denervation of which fiber type?
options: All fiber types about equally, with no preferential loss
Type I (slow-twitch) fibers, explaining the early decline in endurance
Type II (fast-twitch) fibers, explaining the disproportionate decline in power
questions.explanation: Sarcopenia involves atrophy driven by inactivity and a gradual, selective denervation of Type II (fast-twitch) fibers. This preferential loss of fast-twitch tissue explains the disproportionate decline in muscle power with aging, rather than an equal or Type I-selective loss.

questions.question: Because NADH and FADH2 hand off their electrons at different entry points along the electron transport chain, they do not pump the same number of protons and so yield different amounts of ATP. Using the current biochemistry values, how do their per-molecule ATP yields compare?
options: One NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and one FADH2 about 1.5 ATP
One NADH yields about 1.5 ATP and one FADH2 about 2.5 ATP
One NADH and one FADH2 yield the same amount of ATP because both ultimately reduce oxygen
questions.explanation: Because NADH enters earlier in the electron transport chain than FADH2, one NADH produces about 2.5 ATP while one FADH2 produces about 1.5 ATP. Complete oxidation of one molecule of blood glucose yields roughly 32 ATP. The yields are not equal, and FADH2 does not exceed NADH.

questions.question: A coach tells a parent that an 11-year-old with no prior lifting experience should see meaningful strength improvement over a 12-week supervised program, but wants to set a realistic expectation rather than overpromising. Based on typical findings for untrained preadolescents completing an 8- to 20-week program, which gain should the coach quote?
options: About 70% to 90%, driven mostly by muscle hypertrophy at this age
About 30% to 40%
About 5% to 10%, similar to what a well-trained adult would expect
questions.explanation: Strength gains of roughly 30% to 40% are typically observed in untrained preadolescent children after short-term (8 to 20 week) resistance training programs. These early gains are driven largely by neural adaptations rather than hypertrophy, and 5% to 10% is closer to what a trained adult sees.

questions.question: A coach progresses loads for a 12-year-old and is warned that one skeletal site, unique to the still-growing athlete, must be protected because injury there could disrupt long-bone growth. Which site is the concern, and where is it found?
options: The diaphysis, the mineralized central shaft of long bones
The mature lamellar bone lining the joint capsule
The epiphyseal plate, the growth cartilage near the ends of long bones
questions.explanation: Growth cartilage in children is located at the epiphyseal (growth) plate near the ends of long bones, at the joint surface, and at the apophyseal insertions; damage to it can impair bone growth. The diaphysis is the already-ossified shaft and is not the growth-related concern. This risk is minimized with proper technique, sensible load progression, and qualified instruction.

questions.question: A coach comparing average strength between male and female athletes notices the sex-related gap is not uniform across the body. When designing a female athlete's program to offset this, which region generally warrants the most added emphasis because the relative deficit versus males is largest there?
options: The upper body
The lower body, where the relative deficit versus males is greatest
Grip strength specifically, with the rest of the body essentially equal
questions.explanation: Sex-related strength differences are most apparent in the upper body; the lower-body gap is comparatively smaller, especially when strength is expressed relative to body mass or lean mass. Program design for female athletes therefore often emphasizes upper body strength development.

questions.question: A cyclist finishing a long, low-intensity ride is drawing an increasing share of ATP from stored fat. Before the triglycerides in her fat cells can be oxidized, they must first be cleaved into free fatty acids and glycerol. Which enzyme catalyzes that initial breakdown?
options: Phosphofructokinase, the rate-limiting enzyme that mobilizes stored fat
Hormone-sensitive lipase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase, which prepares the fatty acids to enter the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Triglycerides stored in fat cells are broken down by hormone-sensitive lipase into free fatty acids and glycerol; the free fatty acids then travel to muscle and undergo oxidation to resynthesize ATP. Pyruvate dehydrogenase acts on pyruvate (a carbohydrate-pathway intermediate), and phosphofructokinase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, not fat mobilization.

questions.question: An S and C professional is setting safety guidelines for a healthy, resistance-training adult over 65. Which single recommendation best fits the guidance for this population?
options: Cue a sustained Valsalva maneuver on every working set to maximize trunk stability
Test a true 1RM every session so progress can be tracked precisely
Generally avoid the Valsalva maneuver, since the blood pressure spike and dizziness it produces raise fall risk
questions.explanation: For older adults, the Valsalva maneuver should generally be avoided because it spikes blood pressure and can cause dizziness, raising fall risk; training should also use pain-free ranges and allow longer recovery. Routine maximal 1RM testing every session is inappropriate given the added risk and recovery demands.

questions.question: A novice must consciously talk himself through each part of a new clean, while a veteran executes it automatically with a quiet mind and spare attention for the environment. In Fitts and Posner's model, these two performers sit at which ends of the learning sequence, first to last?
options: Cognitive stage (early) and autonomous stage (late)
Associative stage (early) and cognitive stage (late)
Autonomous stage (early) and associative stage (late)
questions.explanation: Fitts and Posner describe three stages in order: the cognitive stage (effortful, conscious regulation of movement), then the associative stage (refinement), then the autonomous stage (automatic performance with a relaxed mind). The novice is in the cognitive stage and the veteran in the autonomous stage.

questions.question: A sport psychologist maps an athlete's focus on two crossed dimensions, one running internal to external and the other running broad to narrow, and argues performance depends on matching the right focus to the task. This two-dimensional framework is best identified as:
options: Catastrophe theory, describing a sudden performance collapse
Attentional styles, defined by direction (internal-external) and width (broad-narrow)
The inverted-U model, relating arousal to performance
questions.explanation: The concept of attentional styles holds that focus varies along two dimensions, direction (internal versus external) and width (broad versus narrow), and that matching style to task demands is key. The inverted-U model and catastrophe theory both concern arousal-performance relationships, not attentional direction and width.

questions.question: A coach separates two things in a lifter: a stable personality tendency to read many situations as threatening, versus the specific apprehension the lifter feels in the moments before a max attempt. The stable, dispositional tendency is termed:
options: State anxiety
Eustress
Trait anxiety
questions.explanation: Trait anxiety is a personality variable, the disposition to perceive a wide range of situations as threatening. State anxiety is the moment-to-moment apprehension felt in a specific situation, and eustress is a positive stress response, not the stable dispositional trait.

questions.question: Two lifters walk into a meet: one is nearly asleep and flat, the other is frantically over-hyped and shaky. According to the inverted-U theory, how does arousal relate to their expected performance?
options: Performance improves as arousal rises to an optimal level, then declines with any further increase
Performance climbs continuously and linearly the more aroused an athlete becomes
Arousal and performance have no consistent relationship
questions.explanation: The inverted-U theory holds that arousal facilitates performance up to an optimal point, beyond which additional arousal is associated with declining performance. Both under-arousal (flat) and over-arousal (frantic) sit below the peak of the curve.

questions.question: A coach must psych up an athlete before a simple, well-drilled max deadlift, but calm a different athlete who is still learning a complex, attention-heavy new skill. Regarding the optimal arousal point for each, which statement is correct?
options: Optimal arousal is the same regardless of skill complexity or the athlete's experience
The optimal arousal point is lower for the complex skill and for the less-skilled performer
The optimal arousal point is higher for the complex skill and for the less-skilled performer
questions.explanation: The optimal arousal point is lower for less-skilled athletes and for complex skills, because worrisome thoughts compete for the limited attentional capacity already occupied by movement details. Coaches should lower arousal for novices and complex tasks and may raise it for simple, well-learned skills.

questions.question: During a heavy pull, a lifter silently repeats "chest up, drive the floor" to himself to hold a key technical point of the lift. Classifying self-talk as positive, negative, or instructional, this cue is best labeled as:
options: Positive (motivational) self-talk
Negative self-talk
Instructional self-talk
questions.explanation: Self-talk is generally categorized as positive, negative, or instructional. Instructional self-talk directs attention to the technical, task-relevant elements of the skill ("chest up, drive the floor"), whereas positive (motivational) self-talk is encouraging ("I can do this") and negative self-talk is self-critical.

questions.question: A sidelined athlete who cannot physically train is guided to vividly rehearse flawless performances of her event using all her senses. Which of the following is a genuine advantage that this imagery offers over real practice?
options: The outcome is fully under her control, so she can repeatedly experience success
It reproduces the same outcome uncertainty she would face in real competition
It lets her rehearse without engaging any of the senses
questions.explanation: Imagery is a cognitive skill in which the athlete creates or re-creates an experience using all the senses. A key advantage is that successful performance is entirely under the athlete's control during imaging, whereas reality always carries uncertainty of outcome. Imagery deliberately uses the senses rather than removing them.

questions.question: Before competition, an athlete works through her body one muscle group at a time, deliberately tensing then releasing each, to regulate both mental and physical arousal via control of skeletal muscle tension. This technique is:
options: Systematic desensitization to a feared stimulus
Progressive muscle relaxation
Autogenic training, which uses self-suggestions of warmth and heaviness
questions.explanation: Progressive muscle relaxation self-regulates psychological and physical arousal through deliberate tensing and releasing of skeletal muscle, and can be paired with diaphragmatic breathing. Autogenic training instead relies on self-statements of warmth and heaviness, and systematic desensitization is a fear-reduction procedure, not tension cycling.

questions.question: After a change-of-direction drill, a coach gives one athlete only her stopwatch time, and gives another a breakdown of how her hips and torso collapsed during the cut. The stopwatch time is knowledge of results; the description of the movement pattern is best termed:
options: Knowledge of results
Intrinsic feedback that the athlete senses on her own
Knowledge of performance
questions.explanation: Augmented feedback splits into knowledge of results, information about the outcome relative to the goal (the drill time), and knowledge of performance, information about the movement pattern itself (hip and torso position during the cut). Intrinsic feedback is what the athlete perceives directly, not information the coach supplies.

questions.question: Rather than having athletes finish all reps of one jump before starting the next, a coach shuffles several different jump skills into an unpredictable order within a single session. This arrangement is called:
options: Random practice
Blocked practice
Massed practice
questions.explanation: In random practice, multiple skills are practiced in an interleaved, unpredictable order within a session, in contrast to blocked practice, in which one skill is repeated many times before moving on. Massed practice refers to short or absent rest between attempts (a work-to-rest dimension), not the ordering of skills.

questions.question: While teaching a complex new skill, a coach tells the athlete after each rep only whether the attempt met the goal (correct or not correct), without describing how the movement looked. This augmented feedback is:
options: Intrinsic feedback
Knowledge of results
Knowledge of performance
questions.explanation: Knowledge of results gives information about the outcome of the movement relative to the goal (whether it was correct), whereas knowledge of performance describes how the movement pattern was carried out. Intrinsic feedback is sensed by the athlete directly rather than provided by the coach.

questions.question: A coach debates whether to correct errors mainly by punishing mistakes or by reinforcing correct actions. Per sport psychology guidance, what is the primary reason reinforcement is generally preferred over punishment?
options: Punishment builds skills faster than reinforcement and carries no meaningful downside
Reinforcement is effective only with elite athletes, so it is the safer default
Punishment floods limited attention with task-irrelevant thoughts like fear of failure, while reinforcement directs attention to task-relevant cues and what to do correctly
questions.explanation: Reinforcement helps athletes attend to task-relevant cues and what to do correctly, whereas punishment tends to flood limited attentional capacity with task-irrelevant cognitions such as fear of failure. Reinforcement is therefore generally preferred, and it is effective across skill levels, not only with elite athletes.

questions.question: An athlete training in the heat is told to drink enough during exercise that his body weight loss stays below the threshold at which performance suffers and heat illness risk climbs. Fluid-related body weight loss during exercise should not exceed roughly:
options: 2% of body weight
5% of body weight
8% of body weight
questions.explanation: Athletes should drink enough during exercise to keep water weight losses under about 2% of body weight, which helps prevent overheating, dehydration, and heat illness while protecting performance. Losses of 5% or more represent substantial dehydration well beyond the recommended limit.

questions.question: An athlete asks about a widely studied, legal ergogenic aid found in coffee and tea that helps both endurance and resistance athletes, but is regulated in a category distinct from most dietary supplements. Which substance fits, and how is it classified?
options: Sodium chloride, classified as a stimulant drug
Caffeine, which is classified as a drug rather than a dietary supplement
Creatine monohydrate, classified as a drug rather than a dietary supplement
questions.explanation: Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant found in coffee, tea, soft drinks, and chocolate and is popular with both aerobic endurance and resistance athletes; unlike most dietary supplements, it is categorized as a drug. Creatine is regulated as a dietary supplement, and sodium chloride is a dietary mineral, not a stimulant drug.

questions.question: An athlete tracking intake wants to convert grams of each macronutrient into calories. Which set of energy values is correct?
options: Carbohydrate 4, protein 9, fat 9 kcal per gram
Carbohydrate 7, protein 4, fat 4 kcal per gram
Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate and protein each provide approximately 4 kcal per gram, while fat provides approximately 9 kcal per gram because fats carry more carbon and hydrogen relative to oxygen. Protein is 4, not 9, kcal per gram (the 7 kcal/g figure belongs to alcohol, not a macronutrient here).

questions.question: A coach wants a nutritional strategy that raises the muscle's capacity to buffer or neutralize the hydrogen ions that accumulate during repeated high-intensity efforts. Which pairing works primarily through that buffering mechanism?
options: Beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate
Caffeine and creatine monohydrate
Vitamin C and iron
questions.explanation: Improving buffering capacity through beta-alanine (which raises intramuscular carnosine) and sodium bicarbonate (an alkalinizing agent) can aid performance in activities limited by hydrogen ion buildup. Caffeine acts as a CNS stimulant and creatine works through the phosphagen system, while vitamin C and iron have no primary acid-buffering role.

questions.question: Three athletes ask whether carbohydrate loading is worth it: a marathoner, a 100 m sprinter, and a powerlifter. Carbohydrate loading is most likely to improve performance for which one?
options: The powerlifter, performing single maximal-strength attempts
The marathoner, whose continuous event runs well beyond about 90 minutes
The 100 m sprinter, whose maximal effort lasts under about 10 seconds
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate loading raises pre-event muscle glycogen and benefits continuous aerobic endurance events lasting longer than about 90 minutes (distance running, road cycling, cross-country skiing), where glycogen depletion would otherwise limit late-event performance. It does little for brief, high-power efforts like sprints or maximal lifts, which rely on the phosphagen system.

questions.question: A coach is selecting a sports drink for an athlete training in the heat and wants the electrolyte and carbohydrate content to match the recommended composition. Which option fits?
options: 60 mEq sodium and 30 mEq potassium per liter, with about 1% carbohydrate
No added sodium or potassium, with about 25% carbohydrate
20 to 30 mEq sodium and 2 to 5 mEq potassium per liter, with 5% to 10% carbohydrate
questions.explanation: The optimal sport drink contains 20 to 30 mEq of sodium and 2 to 5 mEq of potassium per liter, with carbohydrate at a 5% to 10% concentration. Very high electrolyte loads or a 25% carbohydrate concentration slow gastric emptying and can worsen, not aid, hydration.

questions.question: An athlete weighing anabolic-androgenic steroid use asks you to state the documented health risks accurately. Which option correctly describes adverse effects associated with anabolic steroid abuse?
options: Increased risk of liver tumors and liver damage, unfavorable blood lipid changes, and elevated blood pressure
An improved cholesterol profile alongside lowered blood pressure
No documented effect on either the liver or the cardiovascular system
questions.explanation: Documented adverse effects of anabolic steroid abuse include hepatic effects such as increased risk of liver tumors and liver damage, plus cardiovascular effects including unfavorable lipid profile changes and elevated blood pressure, along with endocrine and psychological effects. Steroids worsen, not improve, the lipid profile and blood pressure.

questions.question: Immediately after a heavy resistance session, a healthy younger adult wants the post-training feeding that best drives muscle protein synthesis. Which recommendation fits that acute window?
options: At least 100 grams of protein, regardless of the source
About 20 to 50 grams of a high-quality, high-leucine protein
About 3 to 5 grams of protein from any source
questions.explanation: After resistance training, younger individuals should consume about 20 to 50 grams (roughly 8.5 to 20 grams of essential amino acids) of a high-quality, high-leucine protein to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis; older adults may need 40 grams or more. A few grams is too little to maximize the response, and 100+ grams offers no added synthesis benefit for a single feeding.

title: Practical and Applied - Exam One
description: Program Design, Exercise Technique, Implementation and Admin. Section 2.

questions.question: You are profiling a Division I athlete for the off-season and decide her primary resistance training goal is strength/power. Why should you commit to ONE primary training outcome per training block rather than chasing strength and muscular endurance at the same time?
options: Concentrating on one outcome per block (emphasis/de-emphasis) lets you give a sufficient, focused stimulus while still maintaining other qualities, instead of diluting the adaptation
Training two qualities at once is biomechanically impossible because the load-repetition relationship only allows a single rep range
Insurance and liability rules prohibit programming more than one fitness characteristic in a block
questions.explanation: The book recommends concentrating on only one training outcome per block using an emphasis/de-emphasis approach, while still providing enough stimulus to maintain other qualities for later blocks.

questions.question: A beginner client just started training and you are choosing which exercises to prioritize. Why do CORE exercises receive priority over assistance exercises when selecting exercises?
options: Because assistance exercises are unsafe for beginners and must be removed entirely
Because core exercises recruit large muscle areas, involve two or more primary joints, and have greater dynamic correspondence (transfer) to sport movements
Because core exercises always use lighter loads, making them easier to coach first
questions.explanation: Core exercises recruit one or more large muscle areas and involve multiple primary joints, giving them direct application and dynamic correspondence to sport; that's why they're prioritized.

questions.question: An athlete's session includes a power clean, a back squat, a barbell row, and biceps curls. Following the recommended exercise order, where should the power clean go and why?
options: Last, so accumulated fatigue forces greater motor-unit recruitment
First, because power exercises place a large neuromuscular and skill demand and are prone to fatigue, so the athlete should perform them while metabolically fresh
It doesn't matter; exercise order has no documented effect on adaptation
questions.explanation: Power exercises are performed first because of their high neuromuscular and skill demand and proneness to fatigue; doing them fresh protects technique and reduces injury risk.

questions.question: You program a core exercise for a trained athlete with a goal of maximal muscular strength. Which load-and-rep prescription fits?
options: About 67-80% of 1RM for 8-12 reps
Less than or equal to 67% of 1RM for 12 or more reps
Greater than or equal to 85% of 1RM for 6 or fewer reps
questions.explanation: Per table 18.11, strength training in core exercises uses loads of >=85% 1RM for <=6 goal reps; the heavier the load, the fewer reps possible.

questions.question: A hypertrophy-focused athlete is doing a multijoint exercise (e.g., back squat) and a single-joint assistance exercise (e.g., lateral raise) in the same session. How should rest periods differ between the two?
options: Both get the same 30-second rest because they share the hypertrophy goal
The multijoint exercise gets ~2-3 min while the single-joint exercise gets ~60-90 s, because rest is set by relative load and muscle mass involved
The single-joint exercise needs longer rest (3-5 min) because isolation work is more fatiguing
questions.explanation: Hypertrophy rest is ~2-3 min for multijoint and 60-90 s for single-joint work; rest is allocated by relative load and amount of muscle mass, not just the overall training goal.

questions.question: You assigned 3 sets of 6 reps in the bench press. After a few weeks the athlete completes 8 reps in the last set on two consecutive workouts. Per the 2-for-2 rule, what should you do?
options: Increase the load for that exercise at the next training session
Keep the load the same but add two more sets
Drop the load by 10% to manage accumulated fatigue
questions.explanation: The 2-for-2 rule: if the athlete can perform 2 or more reps over the goal in the last set for two consecutive workouts, add weight to that exercise next session.

questions.question: During a depth jump, an athlete pauses noticeably on the ground between landing and the next jump. What happens to the stretch-shortening cycle if this amortization (coupling) phase lasts too long?
options: More elastic energy is stored, making the subsequent jump higher
The stored elastic energy dissipates as heat and the stretch reflex won't enhance concentric force
The Golgi tendon organ is desensitized, increasing force output
questions.explanation: If the amortization phase is too long, the elastic energy stored during the eccentric phase is lost as heat and the stretch reflex no longer augments the concentric muscle action.

questions.question: On the continuum of plyometric drills, which of the following is correctly ordered from LOWEST to HIGHEST intensity?
options: Depth jumps, box jumps, jumps in place, skips
Skips (jumps in place), standing jumps, box jumps, depth jumps
Box jumps, depth jumps, multiple hops, standing jumps
questions.explanation: The intensity continuum runs from low-intensity drills like skips/jumps in place up through standing jumps and box jumps to depth jumps (highest); as intensity rises, volume should fall.

questions.question: You are prescribing lower-body plyometric volume for a beginner (no experience) doing low-intensity drills. Volume is counted in foot contacts per session. Which range is appropriate for that beginner?
options: Around 80 to 100 foot contacts
Around 120 to 200 foot contacts
Around 100 to 120 foot contacts
questions.explanation: Per table 19.6, a beginner at low intensity is prescribed roughly 80-100 foot contacts; higher experience and intensity levels permit different volumes, and beginners are not recommended at high intensity.

questions.question: A 235-pound athlete wants to add high-box depth jumps. What is the appropriate caution, and what is the maximal practical depth-jump box height for effective, safe performance?
options: No cautions apply to heavier athletes; depth jumps up to 60 in. (152 cm) are recommended for everyone
Athletes over 220 lb (100 kg) should approach high-intensity plyometrics and depth jumps from heights >18 in. (46 cm) with caution; a box of about 48 in. (122 cm) is roughly the upper effective limit
