Athletes over 220 lb should only ever use boxes taller than 48 in. (122 cm) to overload the tissues
questions.explanation: Athletes weighing over 220 lb (100 kg) should be cautious with high-intensity plyometrics and depth jumps from boxes higher than 18 in.; about 48 in. (122 cm) is near the maximal effective/safe depth-jump height before technique breaks down.

questions.question: A coach wants to improve an athlete's maximal sprinting speed. Sprint speed is the product of which two variables, and what ultimately underpins maximizing both?
options: Stride length and stride (step) frequency, both underpinned by rapid force production into the ground
Reaction time and arm-swing amplitude, underpinned by flexibility
Ground contact time and body mass, underpinned by aerobic capacity
questions.explanation: Running velocity is a product of step length and step frequency, and the underlying component to maximizing both is rapid force production applied to the ground.

questions.question: An athlete tries to run faster by deliberately reaching out and overstriding. Why does overstriding HURT sprint performance?
options: It increases ground contact time, which dampens the stretch-shortening cycle and lowers step frequency
It shortens ground contact time so much that the athlete can't produce force
It increases step frequency but reduces stride length below optimal
questions.explanation: Overstriding attempts to gain speed via larger ground contact times, which dampens the SSC and lowers step frequency; success comes from high vertical force in a short contact time.

questions.question: You add overspeed (assisted) sprint training such as towing or downhill running for an advanced athlete. What is the recommended ceiling on the speed increase, and a key drawback?
options: Increases should be limited to <=10%; assisted sprinting can cause chop steps and undesirable braking/overstriding mechanics
Increases should reach 25-30%; there are no documented technique drawbacks
There is no recommended limit; assisted work always improves propulsive force
questions.explanation: Assisted/overspeed increases should be limited to <=10%; pushing beyond can prematurely rush the stance phase, reduce muscle activation/propulsive force, and produce chop steps, leaning back, and overstriding.

questions.question: Agility differs from simple change-of-direction (COD) ability. What added component defines AGILITY?
options: A predetermined movement pattern executed at maximal speed
A perceptual-cognitive component (responding to a stimulus) combined with change-of-direction ability
Purely greater eccentric strength with no cognitive demand
questions.explanation: COD is a planned change of direction; agility additionally requires perceptual-cognitive ability, changing direction/velocity/mode in response to a stimulus.

questions.question: An advanced runner needs work just at race pace to improve lactate threshold and the maximal lactate steady state. Which aerobic endurance method is built around an intensity at or slightly above race pace, corresponding roughly to MLSS?
options: Long, slow (extensive endurance) training
Pace/tempo (threshold) training
Fartlek training
questions.explanation: Pace/tempo (threshold) training uses an intensity at or slightly higher than race pace, corresponding approximately to MLSS, to improve running economy, LT, and MLSS.

questions.question: You program classic interval training for a runner. Work intervals close to VO2max typically last 3-5 minutes; what work-to-rest ratio is recommended for those intervals?
options: About 1:3, with rest three times the work duration
About 1:1, with the rest interval equal to the work interval
About 3:1, with work three times the rest duration
questions.explanation: For 3- to 5-minute interval work bouts near VO2max, the rest interval should equal the work interval, keeping a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio.

questions.question: A swimmer's coach wants variety and asks you to describe Fartlek training. Fartlek is best characterized as which of the following?
options: A combination of extensive endurance, pace/tempo, and interval-type efforts (speed play) that challenges all body systems
Continuous training at a single fixed intensity below the lactate threshold
Maximal sprints with full passive recovery and no aerobic component
questions.explanation: Fartlek ('speed play') blends extensive endurance with bursts of pace/tempo and interval-type efforts, challenging all systems and helping raise VO2max, LT, economy, and fuel use.

questions.question: An athlete under heavy psychoemotional and occupational stress keeps getting more intense training. Per Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome, prolonged excessive stress pushes the athlete toward which phase, associated with overreaching/overtraining?
options: The alarm phase
The resistance (adaptation) phase
The exhaustion phase
questions.explanation: If stress persists too long, the athlete moves into the exhaustion phase of the GAS, where they fail to adapt and most likely experience overreaching or overtraining.

questions.question: You are planning a training block that is several weeks long. On the periodization hierarchy, what is the cycle that typically lasts two to six weeks, with four weeks being the most common duration?
options: Microcycle
Mesocycle
Macrocycle
questions.explanation: A mesocycle lasts several weeks to months (typically 2-6 weeks, most commonly 4); microcycles are usually about a week, and a macrocycle spans months to a year.

questions.question: You are designing the general preparatory (off-season) phase for a strength athlete. In the traditional periodization model, what are the intensity/volume characteristics and primary goals of the hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase?
options: Low-to-moderate intensity, high volume; goals are to build work capacity and muscle mass as a foundation
Very high intensity (50% to >=93% 1RM), very low volume; goal is to peak performance
Maximal intensity (>=85% 1RM), low volume; goal is maximal strength
questions.explanation: The hypertrophy/strength-endurance phase sits early in the preparatory period with low-to-moderate intensity and high volume, building work capacity and muscle mass for later higher-intensity phases.

questions.question: Two programs are compared: Program A keeps reps fixed but rotates heavy/medium/light loads day to day within a week; Program B gradually raises intensity and lowers volume across successive multi-week blocks. What are these two models called?
options: A is the traditional (so-called linear) model; B is daily undulating periodization
A is daily undulating periodization; B is the traditional (so-called linear) model
Both are parallel models with no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: Daily undulating periodization varies the load (and thus volume-load) across days within the week, while the traditional ('linear') model progressively shifts toward higher intensity and lower volume across blocks.

questions.question: A coach builds a warm-up using the RAMP model. In the 'Activate and Mobilize' phase, what is the primary focus that distinguishes it from a traditional static-stretching warm-up?
options: Holding end-range positions statically to lengthen individual muscles
Developing movement competency through key patterns like squats and lunges (mobility, not static flexibility)
Maximally raising heart rate before any skill work
questions.explanation: The 5th edition stresses that the Activate/Mobilize phase targets mobility, the capacity to move actively and effectively through movement patterns, not static flexibility of individual muscles.

questions.question: An athlete needs maximal force and speed output in the activity that immediately follows the warm-up. Which RAMP phase is specifically designed to ramp activity intensity up to competition level and exploit the postactivation effect (treppe/staircase)?
options: Raise
Activate and Mobilize
Potentiate
questions.explanation: The Potentiate phase uses sport- or capacity-specific activities of progressively increasing intensity; the contractile history (treppe/staircase effect) makes the motor neuron more sensitive, improving subsequent high-force, high-speed performance.

questions.question: During a hold-relax PNF hamstring stretch, the athlete performs an isometric contraction of the hamstrings against the partner, then relaxes as the partner increases the stretch. The improved ROM after the isometric is primarily attributed to:
options: Autogenic inhibition
Reciprocal inhibition of the quadriceps
Triggering of the stretch reflex
questions.explanation: Contracting the muscle being stretched (the hamstrings) and then relaxing produces autogenic inhibition, allowing a greater subsequent passive stretch. The stretch reflex is something you avoid, not trigger, during stretching.

questions.question: An athlete uses a fast, bouncing sitting toe-touch where each rep pushes farther than the last. Why does the 5th edition caution that this ballistic approach may limit ROM gains compared with dynamic stretching?
options: It cannot raise muscle temperature
It usually triggers the stretch reflex, which keeps the muscle from relaxing
It only works on the upper body
questions.explanation: Ballistic stretching typically triggers the stretch reflex, preventing the muscle from relaxing, which can limit ROM. Dynamic stretching is controlled and moderate-paced, avoiding the negative effects associated with ballistic work.

questions.question: A spotter is asked to spot a flat barbell bench press (an over-the-face exercise). Which grip should the spotter use on the bar?
options: A closed pronated grip wider than the lifter's grip
A supinated grip matching the lifter's grip width
An alternated grip, usually narrower than the athlete's grip
questions.explanation: For over-the-face barbell exercises the spotter grasps the bar with an alternated grip, usually narrower than the athlete's grip, to safely catch or assist with the load from a higher vantage point.

questions.question: An experienced lifter asks when breath holding (the Valsalva-type strategy) is acceptable rather than the standard exhale-through-the-sticking-point cue. The 5th edition's general breathing guidance is to:
options: Always hold the breath through every set for spinal support
Exhale through the sticking point and inhale during the less stressful phase for most exercises
Inhale during the concentric phase and exhale during the eccentric phase
questions.explanation: For most resistance exercises the athlete should exhale through the sticking point (the hardest part, just after the eccentric-to-concentric transition) and inhale during the less stressful phase. Breath holding is reserved for experienced lifters doing heavy structural exercises.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the five points of the 'five-point body contact' position for a supine bench exercise?
options: Head, shoulders/upper back, buttocks, right foot, left foot
Head, both hands, buttocks, both feet
Shoulders, hips, both knees, both feet
questions.explanation: The five-point body contact position is head, shoulders/upper back, and buttocks firmly on the bench, plus both feet flat on the floor. Maintaining it throughout the lift promotes maximal stability and spinal support.

questions.question: A new lifter wears a weight belt for every exercise, including biceps curls and lat pulldowns. What is the best coaching guidance?
options: A belt is warranted only for exercises that stress the lower back done with near-maximal or maximal loads; overuse limits trunk-muscle training
Belts are appropriate for all exercises to build the habit
A belt should be worn only for upper-body pressing
questions.explanation: A belt is recommended for exercises stressing the lower back during near-maximal or maximal sets. It is not needed for exercises that do not stress the lower back, and wearing it too often reduces training of the abdominal and lower-back muscles.

questions.question: You are coaching a power clean. A trainee asks why you will not have a teammate stand by to 'catch' the bar like on the bench press. The best explanation is:
options: One spotter is always enough for a power clean
The spotter should grasp the athlete's wrists during the catch
Power exercises are not spotted; athletes are instead taught how to miss the lift properly
questions.explanation: Power exercises (e.g., power clean, snatch, jerk) are not spotted because of the safety risk to both athlete and spotter; instead athletes are taught how to miss the lift safely.

questions.question: While watching a deadlift, you see the lifter's hips shoot up faster than the shoulders as the bar leaves the floor. The correct execution is to:
options: Let the hips rise first to protect the knees
Keep the torso-to-floor angle constant so the hips and shoulders rise together, maintaining a neutral spine
Round the upper back to keep the bar closer
questions.explanation: In the deadlift the lifter extends the hips and knees while keeping the torso-to-floor angle constant; the hips should not rise before the shoulders, and a neutral spine is maintained with the bar kept close to the shins.

questions.question: An athlete is performing a two-arm kettlebell swing. Where should the hips and the back be at the bottom of the backswing?
options: Hips flexed with the torso nearly parallel to the floor, back in a neutral spine, elbows extended
Hips fully extended with the back rounded to load the lats
Deep squat with the knees fully flexed and torso vertical
questions.explanation: The kettlebell swing is hip-hinge driven: at the backswing the hips flex until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor with the back neutral and elbows extended; hip extension then propels the bell forward and up to about eye level.

questions.question: A coach watches an athlete flipping a heavy tire and notices the athlete pulling the tire up with the arms (a lifting motion) instead of driving it. Why is this a dangerous flaw the coach should correct?
options: It overloads the hamstrings and stalls the tire at the floor
It is unsafe only because it raises heart rate too quickly
It places greater load on the biceps (risking biceps injury) and the tire can lose momentum and fall back onto the athlete
questions.explanation: Using a lifting rather than pushing motion makes the lifter muscle the tire over, loading the biceps and increasing biceps-injury risk, and the tire can lose momentum and fall backward. The cue is to keep hips low and drive the tire forward, moving with it.

questions.question: When setting up a reverse sled drag (or forward sled pull), what foot position does the 5th edition recommend to maximize horizontal propulsive force?
options: Feet positioned behind the knees with a vertical trunk
The front foot kept in front of the knees while leaning back with a relatively extended hip
Feet together directly under the hips throughout
questions.explanation: For the reverse sled drag the athlete leans back, keeps a relatively extended hip, and keeps the front foot in front of the knees throughout the pull to increase the ability to apply propulsive horizontal forces and accelerate the sled.

questions.question: A strength coach builds a new body-fat assessment device and checks how well its readings line up with same-day DXA scans on the same athletes. What type of validity is being established?
options: Concurrent validity
Predictive validity
Face validity
questions.explanation: Concurrent validity: a new test's scores are correlated with an already-accepted test of the same ability, measured at the same time (this new-body-fat-device-vs-DXA comparison is the textbook's own example of concurrent validity, and 'same-day' is the tell). It is not predictive (that links a score to FUTURE performance). And although DXA is a gold standard, the textbook still classifies validating a new practical test against an accepted test this way as concurrent (criterion validity), not convergent.

questions.question: Two different testers time the same group of athletes in the 40-yard sprint and consistently disagree with each other's recorded times. Which testing quality is lacking?
options: Objectivity (interrater reliability)
Content validity
Intrasubject variability
questions.explanation: Objectivity, also called interrater reliability or interrater agreement, is the degree to which different raters get the same result on repeated occasions. Disagreement between testers points to poor objectivity, often fixed with a clear scoring system and trained scorers.

questions.question: You're sequencing a full test battery for a single session. Following the textbook's logical order, which group of tests should be administered FIRST?
options: Maximum power and strength tests (1RM)
Agility tests like the T-test
Nonfatiguing tests like height, vertical jump, and flexibility
questions.explanation: The principle is that one test must not impair a later one. Nonfatiguing tests (anthropometry, flexibility, vertical jump) come first, then agility, then max power/strength, sprints, muscular endurance, anaerobic capacity, and finally aerobic capacity.

questions.question: An athlete completes the T-test by sprinting forward, then shuffling left, right, and back without crossing the feet, touching cone bases by hand. What ability is this test primarily measuring?
options: Maximal aerobic capacity
Lower-body maximal strength
Change of direction / agility
questions.explanation: The T-test is a change-of-direction (agility) test combining a forward sprint with lateral shuffles in a T-shaped pattern. The best of two trials is recorded to the nearest 0.1 second.

questions.question: A coach wants to estimate an athlete's back squat 1RM from a load-velocity profile instead of testing it directly. What is the recommendation?
options: The load-velocity profile reliably replaces a direct 1RM test
Directly test the 1RM; the load-velocity estimate tends to overestimate the true 1RM
Use the load-velocity profile only for the bench press, never the squat
questions.explanation: When the back-squat 1RM is estimated from a load-velocity profile it is highly variable and consistently OVERestimates the athlete's 1RM, so it should not be used for prediction. Direct testing remains the recommended way to determine maximal strength.

questions.question: A male NCAA Division I athlete's 1RM bench press falls at the 50th percentile on the normative table. How should you interpret this score?
options: Well above average for his group
Average for his group
Well below average for his group
questions.explanation: On the textbook's percentile descriptors, 90 = well above average, 70 = above average, 50 = average, 30 = below average, and 10 = well below average. A 50th-percentile score is simply average relative to the reference group.

questions.question: During rehab from an anterior shoulder dislocation, the athletic trainer asks the S&C coach to begin upper-body strengthening, but notes the bench press should be avoided because it can place the shoulder in a vulnerable position. The bench press is best described as what for this athlete?
options: An indication
A contraindication
A closed kinetic chain exercise
questions.explanation: A contraindication is an activity that is inadvisable or prohibited given the injury. With anterior shoulder instability, the bench press can place the joint in a vulnerable position, making it contraindicated even while other upper-body work is indicated.

questions.question: An athlete reports that the pain from a muscle strain has resolved and wants to return to full play. Based on the tissue-healing model, why should the S&C professional be cautious?
options: Pain often resolves well before tissue healing is complete, so reduced pain does not confirm it's safe to resume
Pain resolution always means the maturation-remodeling phase is finished
Once the inflammatory phase ends, full healing has occurred
questions.explanation: Pain levels typically decrease well before tissue healing reaches the adequate threshold. Athletes may wrongly assume that pain-free means healed, so return-to-play must be judged by healing and objective metrics, not pain alone.

questions.question: A preseason camp deliberately spikes training volume, causing a short-term performance dip, but after a few days to weeks of recovery the athletes supercompensate and perform better than before. This planned process is best termed what?
options: Nonfunctional overreaching
Overtraining syndrome
Functional overreaching
questions.explanation: Functional overreaching is purposely planned overload causing a brief performance decrement that, after short-term recovery (days to weeks), leads to supercompensation and improved performance. Nonfunctional overreaching only returns to baseline, and overtraining requires long-term impairment.

questions.question: When choosing tests for a daily athlete-monitoring program to catch impending overtraining, which category of assessment is most appropriate for everyday use?
options: Category I: easy to administer, inexpensive, rapid turnaround, convenient daily
Category III: occasional, intrusive, expensive, long turnaround
Lab-based endocrine panels run weekly
questions.explanation: Category I tests are daily, easy, inexpensive, and give rapid turnaround (e.g., RPE, resting/recovery HR, HRV, vertical jump), making them suited for routine monitoring. Category III tests are occasional, more intrusive, and slower, so they aren't practical day-to-day.

questions.question: A new strength and conditioning facility is being built. During which phase of the design process is a reputable architect typically hired, usually through a bid process?
options: The predesign phase
The design phase
The construction phase
questions.explanation: The predesign phase consists of a needs analysis, feasibility study, and master plan formation; hiring the architect (often via a low-bid process) is the final step of this phase, before the design phase begins.

questions.question: When planning the total area of a strength and conditioning facility, what is the recommended minimum amount of floor space per individual, counting all athletes, staff, and other persons present?
options: 50 square feet (4.6 m2) per person
100 square feet (9.3 m2) per person
200 square feet (18.6 m2) per person
questions.explanation: The recommended minimum is 100 square feet (9.3 m2) per individual, including all athletes, strength and conditioning professionals, and any additional staff present. Having enough space matters more for the training environment than having extra specialized equipment.

questions.question: A coach is laying out a weight room and wants main walkways that allow safe traffic flow and ADA wheelchair access. What is the recommended width for these main walkways?
questions.explanation: Racks and machines are best lined up in rows running the length of the facility, creating two or three main walkways that should be 5 to 7 feet (1.5-2.1 m) wide. This supports safety, clear access to exits, and ADA-required wheelchair access. (Note: a separate minimum of 3 feet, 0.9 m, applies between individual pieces of equipment.)

questions.question: A facility will program box jumps, vertical jumps, and weightlifting. What ceiling height is recommended to give athletes enough clearance to comfortably perform most of these activities?
questions.explanation: A recommended ceiling height of 12 to 14 feet (3.7-4.3 m) accommodates the athlete plus the space needed for jumping and explosive lifting. Some exercises, like overhead medicine ball throws, may need additional clearance or an alternate space.

questions.question: In the law of negligence, how is the standard of care for a strength and conditioning professional best described?
options: The degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations
The highest level of skill possessed by any expert in the field
Whatever level of care the athlete agrees to in a signed waiver
questions.explanation: Standard of care is the degree of caution and prudence a reasonable person would exercise in similar situations. The strength and conditioning professional is expected to act according to their education, training, and certification.

questions.question: An athlete is recovering from a knee injury and asks the strength coach whether she is medically cleared to resume training. According to scope of practice, who is responsible for providing that medical clearance?
options: The strength and conditioning professional, based on a movement screen
The sports medicine staff (e.g., athletic trainer, physician, or physical therapist)
The athletic director after reviewing the athlete's file
questions.explanation: It is not within the strength and conditioning professional's scope of practice to diagnose or evaluate a medical condition. Only the sports medicine staff can grant medical clearance; the coach then collaborates with them to modify workouts as needed.

questions.question: Per NSCA Strength and Conditioning Professional Standards and Guidelines (Guideline 3.1), which set of recommended professional-to-participant supervision ratios is correct?
options: 1:10 junior high school, 1:15 high school, 1:20 college
1:5 junior high school, 1:10 high school, 1:15 college
1:15 junior high school, 1:20 high school, 1:25 college
questions.explanation: Guideline 3.1 recommends professional-to-participant ratios of 1:10 (junior high school), 1:15 (high school), and 1:20 (college), along with at least 100 ft2 of floor space per participant. Ratios should be increased (more supervision) for complex movements or low-training-age athletes.

questions.question: A strength coach notices a frayed cable on a machine, makes a mental note of it, but does not post an 'Out of Order' sign or remove it; an athlete is later injured using it. This scenario most directly illustrates which legal concept?
options: Assumption of risk
Sovereign immunity
Negligence
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's example of negligence: the coach had a duty to fix the cable or post a sign, breached that duty by failing to act, and that failure proximately caused a foreseeable injury. Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages.

title: Practical and Applied - Exam Two
description: Program Design, Exercise Technique, Implementation and Admin. Section 2.

questions.question: A 22-year-old soccer player joins your program. He has competed at a high level for six years, but his intake questionnaire and a movement screen show only about seven weeks of unstructured lifting and poor barbell technique. Using resistance training status to set his starting point, how should you classify him and prescribe initial frequency and training stress?
options: Advanced; four or more sessions per week at high training stress since he is an elite competitor
Beginner; roughly one to two sessions per week at low training stress while technique is taught
Intermediate; three to four sessions per week at moderate training stress because his years of sport count as training age
questions.explanation: Resistance training status reflects weight room experience and lifting skill, not sport experience or competitive level. Under two months of training with minimal skill classifies an athlete as a beginner, who should start with low frequency (about one to two days per week) and low training stress while learning technique.

questions.question: In a muscular strength program, a lifter finishes a heavy multijoint core lift and then moves to lateral shoulder raises loaded at a 12RM. A newer coach wants to give the raises the same rest the core lift received. What rest length actually fits the lateral raise, and on what basis?
options: At least 5 minutes, because single-joint work still demands full neuromuscular recovery
The same 2 to 5 minutes as the core lift, because the whole session shares one strength goal
About 1 minute, because rest is set by the relative load and muscle mass of that specific exercise, both of which are low here
questions.explanation: Rest between sets is assigned by the relative load and amount of muscle mass involved in each exercise, not by the overall program goal. A light single-joint assistance lift such as a 12RM lateral raise needs only about 1 minute of rest even inside a strength program.

questions.question: A trained athlete's block is centered on maximal strength, and the back squat is the core lift. You want the load and repetition prescription to land squarely in the maximal strength zone rather than drifting toward hypertrophy. Which prescription fits?
options: At least 85 percent of 1RM for about 6 or fewer repetitions
About 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
About 60 to 67 percent of 1RM for 12 to 15 repetitions
questions.explanation: Maximal strength on core exercises is trained with loads of at least 85 percent of 1RM for roughly 6 or fewer repetitions. The moderate-load, higher-rep ranges target hypertrophy and muscular endurance instead.

questions.question: You are building a hypertrophy-focused day around multijoint lifts and want each core exercise's load and rep scheme to sit in the middle of the hypertrophy zone, not bleed into the strength or endurance zones. Which prescription fits?
options: Below 67 percent of 1RM for more than 15 repetitions
About 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for 8 to 12 repetitions
About 85 to 90 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions
questions.explanation: Hypertrophy is emphasized with moderate loads of roughly 67 to 80 percent of 1RM for about 8 to 12 repetitions, balancing mechanical tension against enough volume. Heavier low-rep work targets strength, and very light high-rep work targets muscular endurance.

questions.question: During a power block you are programming for a shot putter, whose event is a single explosive effort. You want the load and rep scheme that maximizes power for a single-effort movement. Which prescription is recommended?
options: About 75 to 85 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions performed explosively
30 to 50 percent of 1RM for 10 to 12 repetitions performed explosively
80 to 90 percent of 1RM for 1 to 2 repetitions performed explosively
questions.explanation: Single-effort power events are trained with about 80 to 90 percent of 1RM for 1 to 2 repetitions performed explosively. Multiple-effort power uses a lower load, about 75 to 85 percent of 1RM, for 3 to 5 repetitions.

questions.question: In a power phase you load the power clean to 80 percent of 1RM. The athlete clearly could grind out five or six reps, but you cap the set at three. A teammate asks why you are leaving reps 'in the tank.' What is the real reason for stopping short?
options: To keep bar velocity high so the set trains power instead of degrading into slow, fatiguing grinding reps
To accumulate the most time under tension possible on each set
To ensure the set reaches muscular failure on a heavy compound lift
questions.explanation: Power development depends on high movement velocity. The earliest reps at a given load are the fastest, so a power set uses fewer reps than the load would allow in order to keep every rep explosive rather than slow and grinding.

questions.question: A cross country runner enters a preseason block whose primary resistance training aim is muscular endurance. You want the core-lift load and rep prescription to match that aim and not slide toward strength or power. Which prescription fits?
options: 85 percent or more of 1RM for 6 or fewer repetitions
67 percent or less of 1RM for 12 or more repetitions
75 to 85 percent of 1RM for 3 to 5 repetitions
questions.explanation: Muscular endurance is trained with light loads of 67 percent or less of 1RM for many repetitions, 12 or more per set. The heavier low-rep options correspond to power and strength goals respectively.

questions.question: To save time, a coach has an athlete perform a set of front squats immediately followed by a set of overhead presses with only brief rest between them, then repeats. A colleague calls this a compound set. What is the method actually called, and what is its main benefit?
options: Circuit training, whose main benefit is maximizing the metabolic conditioning effect
A compound set, which stacks two exercises for the same muscle group to pre-exhaust it
An alternating (push-pull) arrangement, which lets one region recover while the other works and improves time efficiency
questions.explanation: Alternating an upper-body and a lower-body exercise with brief rest is a push-pull (alternating muscle-group) arrangement: one region recovers while the other trains, improving time efficiency. It is not a compound set (two exercises for the same muscle group), and a superset specifically pairs opposing agonist and antagonist muscles.

questions.question: A coach logs a session of 3 sets of 10 back squats at 100 kg and computes the volume-load. A second coach did full-range squats while this athlete used a shortened partial range, yet both logged the identical numbers. What is the volume-load, and what does this measure fail to capture?
options: 3,000 kg; it fails to capture actual bar displacement, so partial and full-range squats show the same value
1,000 kg; it fails to capture the number of sets performed
30 repetitions; it fails to capture the load that was lifted
questions.explanation: Volume-load equals sets times reps times weight, so 3 x 10 x 100 kg is 3,000 kg. Because it multiplies only weight by repetitions, it ignores bar displacement (range of motion), so a partial-range and a full-range squat with the same sets, reps, and load produce identical volume-load.

questions.question: You are prescribing low-intensity lower-body plyometric drills for a beginner and need to record the session's volume in the appropriate unit. How should lower-body plyometric volume be expressed?
options: As the number of sets carried to technical failure
As foot contacts per session
As total minutes of jumping per session
questions.explanation: Lower-body plyometric volume is counted as foot contacts per session, each instance a foot or the feet contact the surface. Bounding drills may instead be quantified by distance covered.

questions.question: You are ordering boxes for depth jumps and box jumps and want a height range that allows a meaningful eccentric stimulus without pushing athletes past the height where landing mechanics break down. Which height range is recommended?
options: 2 to 12 inches (5 to 30 cm)
12 to 60 inches (30 to 152 cm)
6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm)
questions.explanation: Plyometric boxes should range from 6 to 42 inches (15 to 107 cm), with a nonslip top and a stable base. Heights near the top of this range give a large eccentric overload; going much higher tends to break down landing technique and raise injury risk.

questions.question: An athlete is running a circuit-style muscular endurance program with light loads and high repetitions, and you want the between-set rest to reinforce the endurance stimulus rather than allow full recovery. Which rest length fits?
options: 30 seconds or less
2 to 5 minutes
2 to 3 minutes
questions.explanation: Muscular endurance programs use very short rest periods, often 30 seconds or less, to deliberately limit recovery when light loads are lifted for many repetitions. Longer rests correspond to hypertrophy (2 to 3 minutes) and strength or power (2 to 5 minutes).

questions.question: You are setting weekly resistance training frequency for a trained athlete who is currently in the off-season and building a base before the season starts. Based on frequency guidelines by sport season, which weekly range is appropriate?
options: 1 to 3 sessions per week
4 to 6 sessions per week
3 to 4 sessions per week
questions.explanation: For a trained athlete, recommended frequency by sport season is 4 to 6 sessions per week in the off-season, 3 to 4 in the preseason, 1 to 3 in-season, and 0 to 3 postseason during active rest. The off-season allows the highest frequency.

questions.question: A distance runner wants to accumulate time near VO2max to raise aerobic power and asks you to program classic interval training specifically (not HIIT). Which combination of intensity, work-bout length, and work-to-rest ratio defines interval training?
options: Below the lactate threshold, performed continuously for about 30 to 120 minutes
Greater than VO2max, short bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds, roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio
Close to VO2max, work bouts of about 3 to 5 minutes, roughly a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio
questions.explanation: Interval training uses work bouts near VO2max lasting about 3 to 5 minutes at roughly a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio, which lets the athlete accumulate time near VO2max. Greater-than-VO2max short bouts at about 1:5 describe HIIT, and continuous submaximal work describes long slow distance training.

questions.question: A coach is deciding between HIIT and standard interval training and needs to explain how HIIT differs on intensity, work duration, and work-to-rest ratio. Which description correctly captures HIIT relative to standard intervals?
options: HIIT is performed above VO2max with shorter work bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds and roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio
HIIT is performed below VO2max with longer work bouts and about a 1:1 work-to-rest ratio
HIIT uses the same intensity and bout length as interval training but with a much longer relief period
questions.explanation: HIIT uses shorter work bouts of about 30 to 90 seconds at intensities greater than VO2max with a longer relief period, roughly a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio. Standard interval training is near VO2max for about 3 to 5 minutes at roughly 1:1.

questions.question: A coach notes that the back squat loads the spine and requires the lifter to keep a rigid torso and neutral spine so posture is stabilized against the load throughout the lift. Within the exercise classification system, which category best fits the back squat on that basis?
options: A single-joint assistance exercise
A structural exercise
A power exercise, because any barbell squat is defined by explosive intent
questions.explanation: A core exercise that loads the spine directly or indirectly and requires muscular stabilization of posture during the lift is classified as a structural exercise. A structural exercise performed very quickly or explosively is further classified as a power exercise, but a standard back squat is simply structural.

questions.question: A sprint coach is contrasting the low, forward-leaning drive an athlete uses coming out of the blocks with the tall, upright running he does once he has reached full speed. These two portions of the sprint are best labeled as which phases?
options: The braking phase and the recovery phase
The amortization phase and the concentric phase
The acceleration phase and the maximal-velocity phase
questions.explanation: Sprinting requires the ability to accelerate and then reach maximal velocity. The acceleration phase (drive out of the blocks) and the maximal-velocity phase (upright top-end running) use different body positions and produce vertical and horizontal ground reaction forces of differing magnitude.

questions.question: You are outlining the preparatory (off-season) period for a traditionally periodized athlete and need to describe its characteristic training emphasis. Which combination correctly characterizes that period?
options: Low to moderate intensity with high volume, emphasizing hypertrophy and strength endurance
Moderate intensity with sport-specific technique and tactics as the primary focus
High intensity with very low volume and peaking work as the main emphasis
questions.explanation: The preparatory/off-season period uses high volume at lower intensity to build a base, hypertrophy, and strength endurance, with a low technical and tactical emphasis. Intensity rises and volume falls as competition approaches.

questions.question: A team-sport athlete faces a competitive period spanning several months, and the goal is to retain strength and power while managing the fatigue of frequent competition. How is a maintenance program for such a prolonged competitive period generally characterized?
options: Maximal volume and maximal intensity held constant every week to prevent detraining
Moderate to high intensity of about 85 to 93 percent of 1RM at low to moderate volume
High volume at low intensity below 60 percent of 1RM to minimize joint stress
questions.explanation: During a prolonged competitive period, a maintenance program is marked by moderate to high intensity, about 85 to 93 percent of 1RM, at low to moderate volume, with loads modulated microcycle to microcycle around the competition schedule.

questions.question: A coach tapers an athlete before a competition and observes performance rise above baseline in the days that follow. Using the fitness-fatigue paradigm, how is preparedness best described, and why does the taper work?
options: Preparedness is the sum of fitness and fatigue, which rise together and remain permanently elevated after training
Preparedness is the fatigue component alone, so reducing load simply removes fatigue while fitness stays fixed
Preparedness is the fitness component minus the fatigue component; because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, reducing load lets preparedness rise
questions.explanation: Each training bout produces both fitness and fatigue, and preparedness is their net effect (fitness minus fatigue). Because fatigue dissipates faster than fitness, reducing the training load during a taper lets preparedness climb above baseline.

questions.question: A coach wants to make an athlete faster and is deciding what to target in training. Sprint speed is the product of which two variables, and what primarily drives improvement in both?
options: Stride length and stride rate (frequency), improved mainly by applying greater force during the brief ground-contact time
Reaction time and flexibility, improved mainly through static stretching
Body mass and limb length, improved mainly by adding external load
questions.explanation: Sprint speed equals stride length times stride frequency. Faster sprinters direct larger forces into the ground during a brief stance phase, which lengthens the stride while a high stride rate is maintained.

questions.question: Setting up for a heavy deadlift, a lifter positions one hand so the palm faces the body and the other so the palm faces away, specifically to stop the bar from rolling out of the hands as the load gets heavy. Which grip is being used?
options: A neutral grip
An alternated grip
A supinated grip
questions.explanation: An alternated grip places one hand pronated (palm facing away) and the other supinated (palm facing the body). It is commonly used on heavy pulling movements such as the deadlift to keep the bar from rolling and improve grip security.

questions.question: Working through a RAMP warm-up, a coach reaches the final segment right before performance and uses specific, increasingly intense movements at competition intensity to exploit a postactivation potentiation effect. Which RAMP phase is this?
options: Activate and Mobilize
Raise
Potentiate
questions.explanation: The Potentiate phase uses specific, progressively more intense movements to bring activity up to competition intensity and take advantage of postactivation potentiation right before the main activity. Raise elevates body temperature and heart rate early, and Activate and Mobilize targets key muscles and ranges of motion in between.

questions.question: An athlete asks whether adding a block of static stretching to the pre-competition warm-up will help him jump and sprint better. How is the current evidence on static stretching in a warm-up best summarized with respect to subsequent performance?
options: It is equivocal, and several reviews suggest it can compromise force and power performance
It reliably improves force and power output when done before performance
It has been shown to have no measurable effect on any performance variable
questions.explanation: The literature on static stretching in warm-ups is equivocal, and a number of reviews report negative effects on force production and power. That is why dynamic warm-ups are generally favored before performance.

questions.question: A coach is explaining how to execute the concentric phase of a power clean and, separately, what training through a full range of motion does to flexibility. Which statement is correct on both counts?
options: Flexibility is unaffected by full-ROM training, and the concentric phase of an explosive lift should follow a fixed 3-second tempo
Flexibility is maintained or improved through full-ROM training, and the concentric phase of an explosive lift should be accelerated to maximal speed while keeping control and form
Flexibility decreases with full-ROM training, so the concentric phase of an explosive lift should be slowed deliberately to protect the joint
questions.explanation: Training through a full range of motion maintains or even improves flexibility. For explosive movements such as the power clean, the bar should be accelerated to maximal speed during the concentric phase while control and proper form are maintained.

questions.question: Checking a lifter's hand placement on the bar, you see the thumb resting alongside the fingers on the same side of the bar rather than wrapped around it. You correct it to a closed grip. Why is wrapping the thumb around the bar preferred over that open or false grip?
options: It is only necessary for supinated grips and can be skipped on pronated grips
It increases the range of motion available at the wrist during the lift
It keeps the bar from slipping out of the hands, improving control and safety
questions.explanation: In a closed grip the thumb is wrapped around the bar, securing it in the hand. In an open or false grip the thumb sits alongside the fingers, which allows the bar to slip out more easily and is less safe, regardless of whether the grip is pronated or supinated.

questions.question: You are spotting an athlete doing heavy dumbbell chest presses. During the last rep her elbows begin to buckle and the dumbbells drift toward her face and chest. To have the best chance of stopping the weights before they strike her, where should your hands already be positioned?
options: At her wrists or on the forearms just below the wrists
At the elbows, so you can push the upper arms back up as they bend
Under the dumbbells themselves, cupping the plates from below
questions.explanation: Dumbbells are spotted at the forearms near the wrists, closest to the load, so the spotter can actually arrest the weights. Spotting at the elbows leaves the spotter unable to stop the dumbbells from continuing toward the athlete once the elbows collapse.

questions.question: A beginner is setting up for a standard barbell exercise and asks you how far apart to place the hands as a starting default. Absent a specific reason to go wider or narrower, what should you tell him?
options: As wide as he can comfortably reach to increase leverage
Roughly shoulder-width apart
Hands touching in the center of the bar for maximum control
questions.explanation: Grip widths are described as common, wide, and narrow, but the common default for most exercises places the hands approximately shoulder-width apart to keep the load balanced on the bar. Widest-possible or hands-together grips are special cases, not the default.

questions.question: During a training session an athlete asks you to stand behind him and 'catch' the bar on his power cleans the same way you would guide the bar back to the rack on a failed bench press. How should you respond?
options: Position two spotters, one at each end of the bar, to share the load
Agree and prepare to catch, since any lift performed with heavy weight must be spotted
Decline, because explosive lifts are not spotted; the safer approach is coaching him to miss or dump the bar cleanly
questions.explanation: Because of the speed of the movement, explosive lifts such as the power clean are not spotted; a spotter cannot safely intervene and would be endangered. Instead the athlete is taught to miss the lift by dropping or pushing the bar away safely.

questions.question: A single competent spotter can comfortably handle the weight on an athlete's incline press. A newer staff member suggests adding a second and third spotter 'to be safe.' Why is using just the one capable spotter generally the better choice here?
options: Every added spotter is one more person who must sync timing with the lifter and the others, raising the odds of a coordination error
Facility standards prohibit using more than one spotter on any lift
A lone spotter can generate more rescue force than several spotters combined
questions.explanation: When one spotter can handle the load, one is preferred: each additional spotter has to coordinate with the lifter and every other spotter, and each added person increases the chance of a timing or technique error. Multiple spotters are reserved for loads a single person cannot manage.

questions.question: You are correcting an athlete's stance before a set of standing overhead presses done free of any rack or support. Which foot setup gives the most stable base for this ground-based standing lift?
options: A very wide stance with the weight shifted back onto the heels
Feet slightly wider than hip width, with both the heels and the balls of the feet pressing into the floor
Feet close together directly beneath the hips to stack the joints
questions.explanation: Standing free-weight exercises call for the feet slightly wider than hip width with both the heels and the balls of the feet in contact with the floor, creating a stable base. A narrow stance or loading only the heels undermines that base.

questions.question: An experienced lifter with clean squat mechanics plateaus at lockout. You decide to hang chains from the bar for his back squats. What effect are you counting on, and why does his training background matter here?
options: The chains make the bottom heaviest and the top lightest, which makes them ideal for teaching brand-new beginners
The chains keep resistance constant through the range, so any lifter's experience level is irrelevant
The chains load the top of the squat, where he is strongest, and unload the bottom; the added instability means this suits a lifter who already has solid technique
questions.explanation: Chains add resistance near the top of the lift, where leverage and strength are greatest, and unload the bottom, helping match the load to the strength curve. Because the swinging implements add instability, they are appropriate for athletes who already have solid technique.

questions.question: A coach wants to strengthen an athlete's midsection and assumes only dedicated isolation core drills like crunches will do it. Compared with those isolation drills, how do ground-based lifts such as squats and deadlifts affect the anatomical core?
options: They tend to activate the core to a similar or greater degree while training it to stiffen and transmit force through the kinetic chain
They bypass the core almost entirely because the trunk stays rigid throughout
They recruit the core less than isolation work because the bracing limits trunk motion
questions.explanation: Ground-based free-weight lifts activate the core similarly to or more than isolation exercises, and they train the core to stiffen and transfer force through the kinetic chain in a more sport-relevant way than isolation drills do.

questions.question: An athlete asks you to program his heavy squats and cleans on a wobble board and stability ball to 'build more power.' Based on how unstable surfaces affect force production, how should you advise him?
options: It raises force output and is therefore ideal for peak power development
Unstable-surface work tends to reduce force output, so it fits rehab and prehab better than maximizing strength and power
It leaves force output unchanged, so it can simply replace conventional free-weight training
questions.explanation: The nervous system limits force output when the base is unstable, so training on unstable surfaces can markedly lower the force produced. That makes it useful for rehabilitation and prehab but poorly suited to maximizing strength and power.

questions.question: A coach measures an athlete's vertical jump on Monday and again on Thursday under identical conditions, then examines how closely the two sets of scores agree. Any gap between them is treated as measurement error. Which quality of the test is she evaluating?
options: How thoroughly the test covers the components of the ability being measured
How well the test predicts a future performance outcome
How consistently the test reproduces the same score across repeated administrations
questions.explanation: Administering the same test twice under identical conditions and comparing the scores evaluates test-retest reliability, the consistency or repeatability of the measure. The difference between the two sets of scores represents measurement error. Predictive coverage and content coverage are forms of validity, not reliability.

questions.question: A coach builds an 'agility' test as a fully pre-planned course: athletes memorize every cut ahead of time and never have to react to a stimulus. A panel of experts concludes it fails to measure agility as the sport actually demands it. Which quality is most directly missing?
options: The extent to which the test covers the defining components of the ability measured
The degree to which different testers would score it the same way
The consistency of the score when the test is repeated
questions.explanation: Content validity is the expert judgment that a test covers the relevant components of the quality being measured. An 'agility' test with no perceptual-cognitive or reactive component omits a defining part of agility, so content validity is what it lacks. Scorer agreement and repeatability are separate qualities.

questions.question: Before adopting a new fitness battery, a program director convenes sport experts to judge whether the tests collectively cover every relevant physical ability the sport requires, and in the right proportions. Which quality are the experts establishing?
options: Whether the tests simply appear relevant to the athletes at first glance
The extent to which the battery samples all relevant component abilities in appropriate proportions
The degree to which battery scores correlate with an already-accepted test of the same abilities
questions.explanation: Content validity is the experts' assessment that testing covers all relevant subtopics or component abilities in appropriate proportions, which for sport means every ability the sport demands. Correlating with an accepted test is concurrent validity, and surface plausibility is face validity.

questions.question: You are running an athlete through progressively heavier attempts to find her 1RM back squat. She just completed a submaximal warm-up attempt and is a couple of loads away from her likely max. How much rest is recommended before this next non-maximal attempt versus before an attempt that is close to her maximum?
options: At least 5 minutes before non-maximal attempts and about 10 minutes before near-maximal attempts
About 30 seconds before non-maximal attempts and roughly 1 minute before near-maximal attempts
At least 2 minutes before non-maximal attempts and 3 minutes before near-maximal attempts
questions.explanation: For multiple-trial 1RM testing, allow at least 2 minutes of rest between attempts that are not close to the maximum and at least 3 minutes between attempts that are near the maximum. Shorter rests leave residual fatigue; much longer rests are not what the protocol specifies.

questions.question: A testing session pairs a maximal test of the phosphagen system with a maximal test of the anaerobic glycolytic system. To keep fatigue from one from contaminating the other, how much recovery does each respectively require?
options: About 3 to 5 minutes after the phosphagen test and at least 1 hour after the anaerobic glycolytic test
About 1 hour after the phosphagen test and about 3 minutes after the anaerobic glycolytic test
About 30 seconds after each is enough because both are short in duration
questions.explanation: A maximal phosphagen-system test needs roughly 3 to 5 minutes for full recovery, whereas a maximal anaerobic glycolytic test needs at least 1 hour. The glycolytic test's long recovery is why it should be sequenced so it does not fatigue later tests.

questions.question: An athletic trainer is managing an athlete's acute ankle sprain in the first day or two and wants an approach that reflects the current move away from the older PRICE model, which the field revised because strict rest was not producing the best outcomes. Which strategy fits that updated thinking?
options: Applying heat and deep tissue massage to the area on the first day
POLICE: protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, and elevation
Strict immobilization of the joint for no less than two weeks
questions.explanation: The evidence-based shift replaced the 'rest' of PRICE (protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation) with 'optimal loading' in POLICE, because controlled early loading rather than complete rest tends to yield better outcomes and faster recovery. Prolonged immobilization and early heat/massage run counter to this.

questions.question: An athlete tears a muscle acutely and reports pain, swelling, and redness at the site. During roughly what window does this initial healing phase last, and which physiological change is characteristic of it?
options: Roughly six months, characterized by full return of the tissue's original strength
Roughly two months, characterized by realignment of collagen and rising tissue strength
Roughly the first 72 hours, characterized by increased inflammatory cells and decreased collagen synthesis
questions.explanation: The inflammatory response phase typically lasts about 72 hours and is marked by pain, swelling, redness, an influx of inflammatory cells, and decreased collagen synthesis. Collagen realignment and rising strength belong to the later repair and remodeling phases, which unfold over weeks to months.

questions.question: You are guiding an athlete through the early healing phase after a medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain of the knee. Knowing which loading direction most directly stresses that ligament, which type of movement should you avoid for now?
options: Frontal-plane, valgus-loading movement such as a lateral box jump or side shuffle
Closed-chain sagittal loading such as a leg press
Straight-ahead sagittal-plane movement such as an easy jog
questions.explanation: The MCL resists valgus (frontal-plane) stress at the knee, so frontal-plane movements like lateral box jumps and side shuffles load the injured ligament most and are avoided in early healing, then reintroduced in later phases. Straight-ahead jogging and leg pressing do not impose the same valgus stress.

questions.question: A preseason camp deliberately overloads training volume for a couple of weeks. Performance dips briefly, then rebounds above baseline once athletes recover within days to a few weeks. How is this planned response best classified relative to a more severe state that would take weeks to months to resolve?
options: Ordinary acute fatigue that bears no relationship to the overtraining continuum
Functional overreaching, in contrast to nonfunctional overreaching
Overtraining syndrome, in contrast to functional overreaching
questions.explanation: Functional overreaching is intentionally programmed: a short-term performance decrement is followed by recovery within days to weeks and a supercompensation rebound. Nonfunctional overreaching is more severe and takes longer to resolve, and overtraining syndrome involves long-term impairment lasting weeks to months or more.

questions.question: Two athletes are diagnosed with different forms of overtraining syndrome: a powerlifter whose case traces to chronically high training intensity, and a marathoner whose case traces to accumulated high volume. Which mapping of these forms is correct?
options: Both cases are the same condition, since the sympathetic and parasympathetic labels are interchangeable
The powerlifter has volume-driven parasympathetic overtraining; the marathoner has intensity-driven sympathetic overtraining
The powerlifter has intensity-driven sympathetic overtraining; the marathoner has volume-driven parasympathetic overtraining
questions.explanation: Sympathetic overtraining is intensity-driven and more typical of strength and power athletes, whereas parasympathetic overtraining is volume-driven and more typical of endurance athletes who accumulate large training volumes. The two forms are distinct, not interchangeable.

questions.question: You are advising on HVAC setpoints for a new weight room and want athletes comfortable enough to train at a high quality. Which range should you target as the optimal training temperature?
options: 68 to 74 degrees F (20 to 23 degrees C)
58 to 64 degrees F (14 to 18 degrees C)
78 to 84 degrees F (26 to 29 degrees C)
questions.explanation: An appropriate weight-room range is about 68 to 78 degrees F, with an optimal target near 68 to 74 degrees F (20 to 23 degrees C). A room that is too cold or too hot degrades training quality, so both the low-50s/60s and high-70s/80s ranges are outside the recommendation.

questions.question: A facility manager is installing wall mirrors along the dumbbell area and wants to keep dropped or rolling weights from striking and shattering them. What is the recommended minimum height for the bottom edge of the mirrors above the floor?
options: At least 48 inches (122 cm) above the floor
At least 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor
At least 6 inches (15 cm) above the floor
questions.explanation: Mirrors should sit a minimum of 20 inches (51 cm) above the floor so dropped or rolling weights are less likely to strike and shatter them. The 6-inch figure is the separate recommendation for clearance between a mirror and adjacent equipment, not its height off the floor.

questions.question: A facility will train athletes for weightlifting competition and needs regulation lifting platforms. Consistent with competition rules, how should each platform be constructed?
options: As an all-foam matted surface for maximum cushioning
As a single wooden surface across the entire platform
With a wooden middle section and rubber outer sections
questions.explanation: In line with weightlifting competition rules, platforms have a wooden middle section where the lifter stands and rubber outer sections. Inlaid platforms are also preferred over raised ones because they remove a tripping hazard. An all-wood or all-foam surface does not meet the standard.

questions.question: You are laying out a resistance-training area with racks, barbells, and dumbbells and need enough room for both the athlete and a spotter to move safely around each station. What is the minimum recommended spacing between pieces of equipment?
options: 3 feet (0.9 m) between each piece
7 feet (2.1 m) between each piece
1 foot (0.3 m) between each piece
questions.explanation: Racks, barbells, and dumbbells should have at least 3 feet (0.9 m) of space between them so the athlete and spotter can move safely, with additional clearance where multiple spotters are used. One foot is too tight, and 7 feet exceeds the stated minimum.

questions.question: While setting environmental controls for a strength and conditioning facility, you want to hold humidity low enough to limit microbial growth and equipment rust in areas where athletes are active. What upper limit should relative humidity not exceed?
options: It should never drop below 75%
It should not exceed 60%
It should be maintained at exactly 90%
questions.explanation: In any space where physical activity occurs, relative humidity should not exceed 60%. Staying below that level limits bacterial and microbial growth and reduces rust and equipment damage; holding it at 90% or above, or forcing it to stay above 75%, would worsen those problems.

questions.question: An injured athlete sues a strength and conditioning professional, alleging negligence. For the claim to succeed, the plaintiff must prove four specific elements by a preponderance of the evidence. Which set lists those four elements?
options: Liability, insurance coverage, a signed waiver, and proximate cause
Intent, malice, damages, and consent
Duty, breach of that duty, causation, and damages
questions.explanation: Negligence is a tort with four elements: a duty owed, a breach of that duty, causation linking the breach to the harm, and damages, each proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Intent and malice belong to other torts; liability, insurance, and waivers are not the elements themselves.

questions.question: An athlete signed an assumption-of-risk waiver before starting a program. He is later hurt in a way that a court finds was caused by the strength and conditioning professional's negligence. What protection does the signed waiver actually provide in that situation?
options: It may fail to shield the professional from liability, because the injury was caused by negligence
It fully bars any liability, no matter how the professional acted
It shifts all liability onto the supervising athletic trainer
questions.explanation: An assumption-of-risk waiver acknowledges the inherent risks of an activity, but it may not protect the professional when the injury results from negligence. Waivers do not excuse negligent conduct, and they do not transfer that liability to a third party.

questions.question: A high school athlete returning from a concussion asks his strength coach to sign off that he is medically cleared to resume contact practice. Under the NSCA's defined scope of practice for the strength and conditioning professional, what is the appropriate action?
options: Issue the clearance himself so the athlete does not miss training time
Recognize that clearance is outside his expertise and refer the athlete to the appropriate professional
Leave the decision entirely to the athlete's own judgment
questions.explanation: The scope of practice requires the strength and conditioning professional to recognize the boundaries of his expertise and to consult with or refer to the appropriate professional, such as a physician, for matters like medical clearance. Providing clearance personally, or deferring to the athlete, falls outside that scope.

title: Full Mixed Review
description: All seven domains mixed together. A quick full-exam gut check.

questions.question: In the 5th-edition fiber-type classification, which fiber type is described as red, with high myoglobin content?
options: Type IIx (fast-twitch glycolytic)
Type I (slow-twitch oxidative)
Type IIa, but never Type I
questions.explanation: Type I (slow) fibers are RED because of high myoglobin and dense capillaries; Type IIx are white (low myoglobin) and Type IIa are intermediate (white/red). A common mnemonic error is to flip this and call slow fibers 'white.'

questions.question: The complete oxidation of one molecule of blood glucose yields a NET of how many ATP?
options: 38 ATP
32 ATP
4 ATP
questions.explanation: Using current P/O ratios (NADH = 2.5 ATP, FADH2 = 1.5 ATP) the 5th edition lists ~32 ATP net from blood glucose (and 34 from muscle glycogen). The older figure of 38 used the outdated NADH = 3 convention.

questions.question: Glycolysis that begins with muscle glycogen nets more ATP than glycolysis beginning with blood glucose because:
options: Glycogen contains more carbon per molecule
Free glucose must be phosphorylated by hexokinase at the cost of 1 ATP, whereas glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated
Glycogen bypasses the electron transport chain
questions.explanation: Trapping free blood glucose in the cell costs an ATP (hexokinase step). Glycogen-derived glucose is already phosphorylated, so the 5th edition lists 34 ATP from glycogen vs 32 from blood glucose.

questions.question: At the very onset of all-out exercise, which energy system predominates?
options: Oxidative (aerobic) system
Phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system
Fast glycolysis
questions.explanation: The phosphagen system is highly active at the start of ALL exercise regardless of intensity because it resynthesizes ATP fastest (creatine kinase). It has the lowest capacity, so it dominates only the first few seconds.

questions.question: Per the sliding-filament theory, which regions of the sarcomere get SMALLER during contraction?
options: The A-band only
The H-zone and the I-band
Only the A-band, while sarcomere length is unchanged
questions.explanation: As actin slides toward the center, the H-zone and I-band shorten while the A-band (myosin filament length) stays constant. The whole sarcomere shortens.

questions.question: Calcium binding to which protein exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin?
options: Tropomyosin
Troponin
Titin
questions.explanation: Ca2+ binds troponin, which pulls tropomyosin off the active sites so myosin crossbridges can attach. Tropomyosin is the 'door' covering the sites when calcium is low.

questions.question: Most human limb movements, such as the elbow flexion of a biceps curl, operate with which lever type?
options: First-class lever, at mechanical advantage
Third-class lever, at mechanical disadvantage
Second-class lever, at mechanical advantage
questions.explanation: Third-class levers (muscle force applied between the fulcrum and the resistance) are most common in the body and work at a mechanical disadvantage - the muscle produces more force than the load, trading force for speed and range of motion.

questions.question: The maximal force a muscle can exert is most directly proportional to its:
options: Volume
Cross-sectional area
Resting length
questions.explanation: Maximal contractile force is proportional to cross-sectional area (the 2nd power of linear dimensions), not volume (3rd power). That is why, as body size increases, body mass rises faster than strength.

questions.question: At a given velocity, which muscle action produces the greatest force?
options: Concentric
Eccentric
Concentric at high velocity
questions.explanation: Force capability is greatest eccentrically, then isometric, then concentric. Torque can even rise with increasing eccentric velocity, the opposite of the concentric force-velocity relationship.

questions.question: An athlete moves from the first transition period (the strength/power phase) into the competitive period of a traditional periodization model. Compared with the first transition period, training during the competitive period typically involves:
options: Higher training volume and lower intensity to build a work-capacity base
Further increased intensity with decreased volume, plus a sharp rise in sport-specific skill and tactical practice
Roughly the same intensity and volume, held constant to avoid any detraining
questions.explanation: Across the periodization periods, volume falls as intensity rises. Moving from the first transition (strength/power phase: low to very high loads at low volume) into the competitive period, the aim is to further increase strength and power by raising intensity while decreasing volume (peaking can reach >=93% of the 1RM at very low volume), and time spent on sport-specific skills and tactics increases dramatically (5th ed, ch 22). Building a base with high volume and low intensity belongs to the preparatory/off-season period.

questions.question: Which best describes cortisol's role relevant to resistance training?
options: An anabolic hormone that builds contractile protein
A catabolic signal hormone for carbohydrate metabolism, with greater catabolic effect on Type II fibers
A hormone whose main action is suppressing fat oxidation
questions.explanation: Cortisol is the primary signal hormone for carbohydrate metabolism - it promotes gluconeogenesis, raises proteolytic enzymes, and inhibits protein synthesis, hitting Type II fibers hardest. It does NOT suppress fat oxidation (insulin does).

questions.question: In men, testosterone is secreted primarily from:
options: The adrenal medulla
Leydig cells in the testes
The anterior pituitary
questions.explanation: Testosterone comes mainly from the Leydig cells of the testes (also ovaries in women and the adrenal glands), then travels bound to globulin and albumin to target tissues.

questions.question: Which factor has the GREATEST effect on the magnitude of excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC)?
options: Exercise intensity
Time of day
The athlete's standing height
questions.explanation: Intensity has the greatest effect on EPOC, although both higher intensity and longer duration increase it. EPOC is the elevated post-exercise oxygen uptake that restores the body after the oxygen deficit incurred at onset.

questions.question: A consistent fiber-type shift with chronic endurance (or resistance) training is:
options: Type I converting to Type IIx
Type IIx shifting toward the more oxidative Type IIa
Type IIa converting to Type I
questions.explanation: Training shifts fibers from the least oxidative Type IIx toward Type IIa. Detraining can cause a Type IIx 'overshoot.' True Type I <-> Type II conversion is not well supported.

questions.question: The minimal essential strain (MES) that initiates new bone formation is approximately:
options: About one-tenth of the force needed to fracture the bone
Equal to the force needed to fracture the bone
About double the fracture force
questions.explanation: MES is roughly 1/10 of the bone's fracture force. Loading above MES (an osteogenic stimulus) recruits osteoblasts to deposit new bone matrix that mineralizes as hydroxyapatite.

questions.question: Complete oxidation of ONE triglyceride molecule yields approximately how many ATP?
options: Over 300 ATP
Exactly 38 ATP
About 100 ATP
questions.explanation: The 5th edition states a triglyceride (glycerol + three fatty acids) yields 'over 300 ATP.' Notes citing 463 ATP use the outdated NADH = 3 convention.

questions.question: Yerkes-Dodson's inverted-U hypothesis predicts that as arousal increases, performance:
options: Increases continuously (more is always better)
Improves to an optimal point, then declines with further arousal
Is unaffected by arousal level
questions.explanation: The inverted-U: arousal helps performance up to an optimal level, beyond which more arousal hurts it. Drive theory, by contrast, predicts a linear increase with arousal.

questions.question: An athlete's belief in their capability to perform a SPECIFIC task in a SPECIFIC situation is called:
options: Trait anxiety
Self-efficacy
Intrinsic motivation
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is task- and situation-specific perceived capability and influences activity choice, effort, and persistence. Self-confidence is the broader belief that one can perform a desired behavior.

questions.question: Removing an aversive stimulus in order to increase the likelihood of a desired behavior is:
options: Positive reinforcement
Negative reinforcement
Positive punishment
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement increases a behavior by taking away something aversive. Reinforcement (positive or negative) increases behavior; punishment decreases it.

questions.question: Which goal type is most within an athlete's control and the recommended emphasis?
options: Outcome goals, such as winning the event
Process goals, such as executing specific technique cues
Outcome and process goals are equally controllable
questions.explanation: Process goals focus on actions the athlete controls (effort, technique). Outcome goals depend on opponents and others, so they are largely outside the athlete's control.

questions.question: The correct order of Fitts and Posner's stages of motor learning is:
options: Automatic, then associative, then cognitive
Cognitive, then associative, then autonomous (automatic)
Associative, then cognitive, then automatic
questions.explanation: Learners progress from the cognitive stage (effortful, conscious) to the associative stage (refining) to the autonomous/automatic stage (little conscious attention needed).

questions.question: The recommended daily protein intake for STRENGTH athletes is approximately:
options: 0.8 g/kg/day
1.4-2.0 g/kg/day
3.5-4.0 g/kg/day
questions.explanation: Strength athletes target roughly 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day (endurance athletes ~1.2-2.0). The general adult RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day.

questions.question: Which plant-based protein is noted as containing all nine essential amino acids?
options: Rice
Soy
Peanuts
questions.explanation: Soy is cited as the only plant-based source containing all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete protein.

questions.question: A common creatine supplementation protocol is:
options: 2 g/day for 30 days with no loading
A loading dose of ~20-25 g/day (or 0.3 g/kg/day) for ~5 days, then ~2 g/day maintenance
A single 0.3 g/kg dose just before competition
questions.explanation: Loading ~20-25 g/day (0.3 g/kg/day) for ~5 days saturates muscle creatine stores, followed by ~2 g/day (0.03 g/kg/day) maintenance.

questions.question: Sodium bicarbonate works as an ergogenic buffer by:
options: Lowering blood pH to speed glycolysis
Raising blood pH, which increases the gradient driving H+ out of muscle cells
Directly supplying ATP to the muscle
questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate raises blood pH, increasing the pH gradient between inside and outside the cell so H+ leaves working muscle faster. Roughly 0.3 g/kg 60-90 min before high-intensity exercise; it can cause GI distress.

questions.question: The Adequate Intake (AI) for water is approximately:
options: 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women
1 L/day for everyone
5 L/day for men and 4 L/day for women
questions.explanation: Water AI is ~3.7 L/day (men) and ~2.7 L/day (women). A fluid loss exceeding 2% of body weight signals inadequate replacement.

questions.question: The glycemic index ranks a carbohydrate against a reference food (glucose or white bread) assigned a value of:
questions.explanation: GI compares a food's ~2-hour blood-glucose response to a reference food (glucose or white bread = 100). Glycemic load additionally accounts for the amount of carbohydrate per serving.

questions.question: To maximize muscle protein synthesis after resistance training in young adults, the recommended protein dose is about:
options: 5-10 g of any protein
20-25 g of high-quality, leucine-rich protein
60-80 g of protein
questions.explanation: About 20-25 g of high-quality, high-leucine (~2-3 g leucine) protein maximizes MPS in young individuals; older adults may need 40+ g. The 'anabolic window' is heavily debated.

questions.question: A 'core' exercise (as opposed to an assistance exercise) is best defined as one that:
options: Targets the abdominal muscles specifically
Recruits one or more large muscle areas, crosses two or more primary joints, and receives priority
Uses only body weight
questions.explanation: Core exercises recruit large muscle areas across 2+ primary joints (e.g., squat, bench press) and get priority for their direct sport application. Assistance exercises are smaller, often single-joint.

questions.question: For improving power output in exercises that can be heavily loaded, the most effective intensity range is roughly:
options: Always 100% 1RM
