questions.explanation: For heavily loadable resistance exercises, ~75-90% 1RM is most effective/practical for power. Rest 2-5 minutes between sets when training single-effort power.

questions.question: The '2-for-2 rule' directs you to increase load when an athlete can perform:
options: 2 reps over the goal on the last set in 2 consecutive workouts
2 total workouts within 2 weeks
2 sets of 2 reps at a new maximum
questions.explanation: The 2-for-2 rule: if the athlete completes 2 or more reps beyond the rep goal on the last set in 2 consecutive sessions, increase the weight.

questions.question: Order these training cycles from LONGEST to shortest:
options: Microcycle > mesocycle > macrocycle
Macrocycle > mesocycle > microcycle
Mesocycle > macrocycle > microcycle
questions.explanation: Macrocycle (months to a year) > mesocycle (2-6 weeks) > microcycle (several days to ~2 weeks).

questions.question: The preparatory (off-season) period is characterized by:
options: High intensity, low volume, sport-specific work
Low intensity, high volume to build a conditioning base
Peaking with very low volume
questions.explanation: The preparatory/off-season period uses low intensity and high volume to develop a conditioning base, raising the athlete's tolerance for later, more intense training.

questions.question: Complex training takes advantage of postactivation potentiation by pairing:
options: A high-load strength exercise followed by a biomechanically similar explosive/plyometric exercise
Two antagonist exercises back-to-back
Steady-state cardio with static stretching
questions.explanation: Complex training follows a heavy strength exercise with a similar explosive (stretch-shortening-cycle) movement to exploit postactivation potentiation.

questions.question: A frequently cited strength prerequisite before an adult performs lower-body depth jumps is a back-squat 1RM of at least:
options: 1.0x body weight
1.5x body weight
2.5x body weight
questions.explanation: A common guideline is a squat 1RM of ~1.5x body weight before lower-body (depth/box) plyometrics. Depth-jump box heights run ~16-42 in (norm 30-32 in); use <18 in for athletes over 220 lb.

questions.question: The recommended MINIMUM recovery between plyometric training sessions is:
options: 12-24 hours
48-72 hours
A full week
questions.explanation: 48-72 hours between plyometric workouts optimizes adaptation while minimizing injury risk.

questions.question: The defining difference between 'change of direction' and 'agility' is that agility:
options: Is simply slower than change of direction
Adds a response to a stimulus (a perceptual-cognitive component)
Only occurs in a straight line
questions.explanation: Change of direction is pre-planned; agility requires reacting to a stimulus, combining perceptual-cognitive ability with change-of-direction ability.

questions.question: Which is generally considered the BEST single indicator of aerobic endurance performance?
options: VO2max
Maximal lactate steady state
Resting heart rate
questions.explanation: The hierarchy given is maximal lactate steady state > lactate threshold > VO2max as an indicator of aerobic endurance performance.

questions.question: In PNF stretching, the first phase always begins with:
options: A 6-second maximal isometric contraction
An initial ~10-second passive, relaxed stretch
A ballistic bounce at end range
questions.explanation: PNF (hold-relax or contract-relax) always starts with a ~10-second passive relaxed stretch, then the contraction phase, then a longer relax.

questions.question: Relaxation that occurs in the SAME muscle that was just actively contracted (e.g., before stretching it) is called:
options: Reciprocal inhibition
Autogenic inhibition
The stretch reflex
questions.explanation: Autogenic inhibition is relaxation in the same muscle experiencing increased tension (GTO-mediated). Reciprocal inhibition is relaxation of the OPPOSING muscle while the agonist contracts.

questions.question: When spotting a dumbbell chest fly, the spotter's hands should be placed near the athlete's:
options: Wrists
Forearms, close to the elbows
The dumbbells themselves
questions.explanation: Spot the dumbbell fly at the forearms near the elbows - not the wrists and not the dumbbells - for the best control and safety.

questions.question: Interval training to develop the phosphagen (ATP-PCr) energy system uses near-maximal (90-100%) efforts of about 5 to 10 seconds. According to the textbook's interval-training table, the appropriate work-to-rest ratio is approximately:
questions.explanation: The 5th ed interval-training table (ch 3) pairs each energy system with a work-to-rest ratio: phosphagen (90-100%, ~5-10 s) = 1:12 to 1:20; fast glycolysis (15-30 s) = 1:3 to 1:5; fast glycolysis + oxidative (1-3 min) = 1:3 to 1:4; oxidative (>3 min) = 1:1 to 1:3. Short maximal efforts need long rest so phosphagens can replenish, hence the large 1:12 to 1:20 ratio.

questions.question: Compared with a high-bar back squat, a low-bar squat (more forward trunk lean) tends to place:
options: More torque on the knees and less on the hips
More torque on the hips and less on the knees
Equal torque on the hips and knees
questions.explanation: Greater forward lean (low-bar) lengthens the moment arm at the hips, so hip torque rises and knee torque falls. The more upright high-bar squat shifts torque toward the knees.

questions.question: In a test battery, which tests should be administered BEFORE the others?
options: Aerobic capacity tests
Non-fatiguing tests and maximal power/strength tests, before fatiguing anaerobic and aerobic capacity tests
Local muscular endurance tests
questions.explanation: Sequence: non-fatiguing -> agility -> max power/strength -> sprints -> muscular endurance -> fatiguing anaerobic capacity -> aerobic capacity. Fatiguing tests go last so they don't contaminate power and skill measures.

questions.question: Sympathetic overtraining syndrome is MOST associated with:
options: Endurance athletes and high training volume
Strength/power athletes and high training intensity
Beginners only
questions.explanation: Sympathetic OTS is intensity-driven and develops first, more common in younger strength/power athletes. Parasympathetic OTS is volume-driven, more common in endurance athletes, and represents the later culmination.

questions.question: Functional overreaching (FOR) differs from nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) in that FOR:
options: Causes months-long performance loss
Causes a short-term performance dip that can supercompensate into gains after an appropriate taper
Always progresses to overtraining syndrome
questions.explanation: FOR is a short-term (days-weeks) decrement that can rebound into gains after a taper. NFOR is a weeks-to-months stagnation/decrement; overtraining syndrome lasts months or more.

questions.question: During the acute inflammatory phase of tissue healing (first ~2-3 days), the strength coach should:
options: Aggressively load the injured tissue to drive adaptation
Avoid exercise that directly stresses the injured area while maintaining cardiorespiratory fitness and surrounding function
Stop all physical activity completely
questions.explanation: In the inflammatory phase, protect the injured structure (avoid directly stressing it) while maintaining cardiorespiratory fitness and the function of surrounding, uninjured areas.

questions.question: Recommended professional-to-participant supervision ratios tighten for younger athletes. The HIGH-SCHOOL ratio is:
questions.explanation: Junior high 1:10, high school 1:15, college 1:20 (adults/elite can be higher). Younger, less experienced athletes need closer supervision.

questions.question: Which four elements must all be present to establish negligence?
options: Duty, breach of duty, proximate cause, and damages
Intent, motive, opportunity, and harm
Contract, payment, service, and refund
questions.explanation: Negligence = a duty to act, a breach of that duty (failing the standard of care), proximate cause (reasonably foreseeable), and resulting damages.

questions.question: The general planning guideline for resistance-training floor space is approximately:
options: ~25 sq ft per athlete
~100 sq ft per athlete
~400 sq ft per athlete
questions.explanation: Plan for roughly 100 sq ft per athlete in the resistance-training area, with walkways over 36 in (over 48 in in circuit areas) and air exchanged 8-12 times per hour.

title: Hardest Mode
description: 80 original, brutally hard questions covering the toughest concepts and trap patterns the CSCS loves to test. Exam-weighted across all seven domains. Two plausible answers per question - read every word. These are original practice items, not actual exam content, and this site is not affiliated with or endorsed by the NSCA. If you can clear this, the real thing will feel easier.

questions.question: An athlete performs a standing dumbbell biceps curl. At the elbow, the biceps inserts close to the joint axis while the dumbbell is held far out at the hand. To hold the weight static at 90 degrees of flexion, what is true about the force the biceps must produce relative to the weight of the dumbbell?
options: The biceps must produce a force greater than the weight of the dumbbell because the muscle's force arm is shorter than the resistance arm
The biceps produces a force equal to the dumbbell's weight because torque is conserved across the joint
The biceps produces less force than the dumbbell's weight because the elbow gives the muscle a mechanical advantage greater than 1
questions.explanation: The elbow during curling is a third-class lever: the muscle (effort) inserts between the axis and the resistance, so its force arm (moment arm) is shorter than the resistance arm. Mechanical advantage = force arm / resistance arm < 1, so the muscle must produce MORE force than the external load to balance torque. The trap is the third option ('mechanical advantage greater than 1') - third-class levers favor range of motion and speed, not force, so MA is always less than 1 and the muscle is at a force disadvantage.

questions.question: A coach wants to compare the torque produced about the knee at two points in a leg extension. The quadriceps tendon force is identical at both points, but at point A the perpendicular distance from the knee axis to the line of muscle pull is larger than at point B. What does this tell you about the muscular torque at the two points?
options: Torque is greater at point A because torque equals muscle force times the perpendicular distance (moment arm)
Torque is greater at point B because a shorter moment arm concentrates the force closer to the axis
Torque is equal at both points because the muscle force did not change
questions.explanation: Torque = force x moment arm, where the moment arm is the PERPENDICULAR distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. With equal force, the larger moment arm (point A) yields greater torque. The trap is the second option: a shorter moment arm produces LESS torque, not more - 'closer to the axis' reduces the lever, it does not concentrate force. The third option ignores that moment arm, not just force, sets torque.

questions.question: Two volleyball players leave the ground with the exact same takeoff velocity and reach the same jump height. Player 1 used a deep, slow countermovement applying a moderate ground reaction force over a longer time; Player 2 used a shallow, quick countermovement applying a much larger force over a shorter time. Which principle best explains how both achieved the same takeoff velocity?
options: The force-velocity relationship, because higher force always permits a higher movement velocity
The Frank-Starling mechanism, because greater stretch yields a more forceful contraction
The impulse-momentum relationship, because the product of force and time (impulse) equals the change in momentum, and both produced the same impulse
questions.explanation: Impulse (force x time) equals the change in momentum (mass x velocity change). Identical takeoff velocity for the same mass means identical change in momentum, so both jumps required the same impulse - achievable as big force x short time OR smaller force x longer time. The trap force-velocity choice describes the inverse relationship between contraction force and shortening velocity within a muscle, not how two jumpers reach equal velocity. Frank-Starling is a cardiac stretch-tension mechanism, irrelevant here.

questions.question: An athlete performs the lowering (return) phase of a standing cable chest fly: starting with the handles pressed together in front of the chest, the arms open outward to the sides under control until they are wide. During this controlled opening, which muscle action is occurring at the shoulder?
options: The shoulder adductors (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi) contract eccentrically, lengthening under load to control the arms moving into abduction
The shoulder abductors (deltoid) contract concentrically to spread the arms apart
The shoulder adductors contract concentrically to open the arms
questions.explanation: On the return phase the cable resistance is pulling the arms apart (toward abduction), and the prime movers of the fly - the shoulder ADDUCTORS (pectoralis major, lat) - lengthen while still generating force to control that motion, so they work eccentrically. The trap is the deltoid (abductors): they would be the concentric mover if the cable were resisting you in the other direction, but here gravity/the cable open the arms and the adductors brake it. A concentric adductor action would bring the arms back together, not open them.

questions.question: Slow-motion video shows a baseball pitcher's throwing arm during the follow-through, immediately after release: the arm has just rapidly internally rotated to deliver the pitch and must now be decelerated before the shoulder reaches its end range. Which muscles act eccentrically to brake the arm?
options: The external rotators of the posterior rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor), lengthening under load to decelerate the internal rotation
The internal rotators (subscapularis, pectoralis major), eccentrically slowing the arm
The middle deltoid, concentrically abducting the arm
questions.explanation: The forceful motion that launches the pitch is rapid internal rotation, driven concentrically by the internal rotators. Decelerating it falls to the antagonist working eccentrically - the EXTERNAL rotators of the posterior cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor) lengthen under load to brake the arm and protect the joint, which is why posterior-cuff eccentric strength is emphasized in throwers. The trap is the internal rotators: they PRODUCE the internal rotation concentrically, they do not brake it. The deltoid is not the decelerator here.

questions.question: A lifter slowly lowers into the bottom of a back squat under control. At the hip, which muscle action is occurring as the lifter descends?
options: The hip extensors (gluteus maximus, hamstrings) are contracting eccentrically to control hip flexion
The hip flexors (iliopsoas) are contracting concentrically to pull the lifter down
The hip extensors are contracting concentrically to lower the body
questions.explanation: Descending into a squat is hip FLEXION occurring against gravity. Gravity supplies the flexing force, so the muscles working are the antagonists - the hip EXTENSORS - lengthening eccentrically to brake the descent. The trap is the hip flexors contracting concentrically: gravity, not the hip flexors, drives the descent, so the flexors are largely passive while the extensors do the controlling work. Concentric hip extension happens on the way UP, not down.

questions.question: During the first roughly 10 seconds of an all-out sprint relying on the phosphagen system, what happens to intramuscular ATP and phosphocreatine (PCr) concentrations?
options: Both ATP and PCr fall dramatically in parallel
PCr stays nearly constant while ATP is markedly depleted
ATP stays nearly constant while PCr is markedly depleted
questions.explanation: ATP concentration is fiercely defended and stays nearly constant even during maximal effort, because the creatine kinase reaction rapidly rephosphorylates ADP using PCr. PCr is the buffer that gets drained - it can drop substantially in seconds. The trap is picking ATP as the substance depleted: a large fall in ATP would compromise the cell, so the body sacrifices PCr to keep ATP stable. The third option reverses the actual physiology.

questions.question: A strength coach is classifying the dominant energy system for a single effort that lasts about 2 minutes at high intensity (for example, a 800 m run sustained near maximal pace). Which energy system contribution best describes this effort?
options: Almost entirely phosphagen, because the effort is maximal
Almost entirely oxidative, because it lasts longer than one minute
A roughly balanced contribution from fast glycolysis and oxidative metabolism
questions.explanation: Energy system contribution is judged by the DURATION of the effort. Efforts of about 1 to 3 minutes draw on a mix of fast glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, with the crossover occurring within this window. The trap 'almost entirely oxidative' is wrong because the glycolytic system is still contributing heavily near the 2-minute mark - oxidative does not fully dominate until efforts well beyond 3 minutes. Phosphagen is essentially spent after roughly 10 seconds.

questions.question: A basketball point guard repeatedly performs all-out 5-second drives separated by jogging and standing. Generically the sport is 'aerobic' over a 40-minute game, but each explosive drive itself is fueled mostly by which system?
options: The oxidative system, because the overall game is long
The phosphagen system, because each individual burst is very short and near-maximal
Fast glycolysis, because basketball is a power sport
questions.explanation: Classify by the duration of the described action, not the sport label. A 5-second near-maximal burst is fueled predominantly by the phosphagen system. Intermittent sprint sports are anaerobic bursts riding on an aerobic base - the aerobic system helps replenish PCr between efforts, but it does not power the burst itself. The trap 'oxidative because the game is long' confuses total game time with the brief effort. Fast glycolysis would dominate efforts more in the 15 to 30 second range.

questions.question: A coach programs 10-second maximal sled sprints. The training GOAL is to maximize speed and power output on every rep, with each rep as crisp as the first. Which work-to-rest ratio best fits this goal?
options: About 1:3 to 1:5 (short rest), so the athlete trains under fatigue
About 1:1, to keep the session time-efficient
About 1:12 to 1:20 (full recovery, roughly 2 to 3 minutes rest), so PCr is nearly fully restored before each rep
questions.explanation: For a speed and power goal, each rep must be high quality, which requires near-full PCr restoration between efforts - a long work-to-rest ratio of about 1:12 to 1:20 (roughly 2 to 3 minutes rest after a 10-second sprint). The trap is the short 1:3 to 1:5 ratio: that incomplete recovery is deliberately used to train anaerobic/glycolytic CAPACITY (forcing work before PCr refills), which degrades power output - the opposite of a speed-power goal.

questions.question: A different coach uses the same 10-second sprints but now wants to build anaerobic (glycolytic) capacity and tolerance to fatigue, deliberately starting each rep before PCr is fully restored. Which work-to-rest ratio fits this goal?
options: About 1:12 to 1:20, full recovery between reps
About 1:3 to 1:5, incomplete recovery between reps
About 1:25, extended recovery to keep quality high
questions.explanation: An anaerobic/glycolytic CAPACITY goal calls for incomplete recovery, around 1:3 to 1:5, so the athlete begins each rep before PCr fully refills, taxing glycolysis and fatigue tolerance. The trap is the long 1:12 to 1:20 ratio - that full recovery is for a speed-power QUALITY goal and would not stress the glycolytic system the way capacity training requires. Note the same 10-second sprint serves opposite goals depending only on the rest interval.

questions.question: Compared with Type I fibers, Type IIx (fast-twitch) muscle fibers are best characterized by which combination?
options: Higher mitochondrial density, greater fatigue resistance, and slower contraction velocity
Greater capillary density, higher myoglobin content, and faster contraction velocity
Higher force output per cross-sectional area, faster contraction velocity, and lower fatigue resistance
questions.explanation: Type IIx fibers contract fastest, produce high force/power, and fatigue quickly; they have relatively low mitochondrial density, capillarization, and myoglobin. The correct answer pairs fast velocity + high force + low fatigue resistance. The first option describes Type I traits (oxidative, fatigue-resistant, slow). The third option mixes Type I oxidative features (capillary density, myoglobin) with fast velocity, an internally inconsistent trap that cannot coexist in IIx.

questions.question: As an athlete progressively increases the force of a muscle contraction, how does the neuromuscular system grade the force output, according to the size principle?
options: Lower-threshold (smaller) motor units are recruited first, then higher-threshold units are added, and firing rate increases
High-threshold motor units are recruited first because they produce the most force
Individual fibers are partially activated to a degree matching the required force
questions.explanation: By the size principle, motor units are recruited in order of increasing size: low-threshold (small, Type I) units first, then progressively larger high-threshold (Type II) units as force demand rises, with rate coding (increased firing frequency) adding further force. The trap second option reverses recruitment order. The third option violates the all-or-none law - a fiber cannot be partially activated; once its motor unit fires, all of its fibers contract fully, and force is graded by recruitment and rate coding, not partial fiber activation.

questions.question: For the cross-bridge cycle of the sliding-filament model to proceed (attachment, power stroke, detachment, and reattachment), which two things are both required?
options: Calcium ions to expose actin binding sites and ATP to power the stroke and detach the cross-bridge
Calcium ions and lactate, which together drive the power stroke
ATP alone, since calcium is only needed for relaxation
questions.explanation: Excitation releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca2+ binds troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose actin's myosin-binding sites. ATP is then required both to energize the power stroke and to detach myosin from actin so the cycle can repeat. The trap third option is a common error: ATP is needed for detachment AND relaxation, but Ca2+ is essential to INITIATE contraction, not just relaxation. Lactate plays no direct role in the cross-bridge cycle.

questions.question: Two muscles have the same physiological cross-sectional area, but Muscle A has highly pennate fibers at a steep angle while Muscle B has fibers running parallel to the line of pull. What is the trade-off for the pennate Muscle A?
options: Greater maximal force potential but a lower maximal shortening velocity
Greater maximal shortening velocity but lower force potential
Both greater force and greater shortening velocity, with no trade-off
questions.explanation: Pennation packs more sarcomeres in parallel per unit area, increasing physiological cross-sectional area and thus force potential, but the fibers are shorter and angled, reducing maximal shortening velocity and the proportion of fiber force transmitted along the tendon. So pennate muscle favors force over speed. The trap second option reverses this (that describes the longer parallel fibers of Muscle B). The third option ignores the inherent force-versus-velocity trade-off of architecture.

questions.question: Based on the force-velocity relationship of muscle, in which condition can a muscle generate the GREATEST force?
options: During a fast concentric (shortening) action, because speed adds momentum
During an eccentric (lengthening) action against a high load
At its maximal unloaded shortening velocity
questions.explanation: Force capability is highest during ECCENTRIC actions, where a muscle can resist loads exceeding its maximal isometric force; force then decreases as concentric shortening velocity increases, and is lowest at maximal (unloaded) shortening velocity. The trap first option is the classic error - faster concentric shortening actually produces LESS force, not more, per the force-velocity curve. The third option describes the point of essentially zero force production.

questions.question: During the early weeks (first few weeks) of a previously untrained person's resistance-training program, strength often improves substantially before any meaningful change in muscle size. What primarily accounts for these initial gains?
options: Rapid myofibrillar hypertrophy adding contractile proteins
Neural adaptations such as increased motor unit recruitment, rate coding, and synchronization
An immediate rise in resting testosterone concentration
questions.explanation: Early strength gains in novices are predominantly NEURAL - greater agonist recruitment, increased firing rate (rate coding), improved synchronization, and reduced antagonist co-activation - and precede measurable hypertrophy, which becomes the dominant driver only later. The trap is hypertrophy, which lags behind neural changes in the first weeks. A chronically elevated resting testosterone level is not the mechanism for the rapid early improvements.

questions.question: After several months of well-designed aerobic endurance training, which set of cardiovascular and peripheral adaptations would you expect?
options: Increased mitochondrial density and capillary density, a widened arterial-venous oxygen difference, and a rightward shift of the lactate threshold
Decreased stroke volume with a higher resting heart rate to maintain cardiac output
Reduced capillary density but greater reliance on the phosphagen system
questions.explanation: Chronic aerobic training increases mitochondrial number/density, capillary density, and the a-vO2 difference (more oxygen extracted per unit blood), raises maximal stroke volume (lowering resting heart rate), and shifts the lactate threshold to the right (higher intensity before lactate accumulates). The trap second option is backward - stroke volume INCREASES and resting heart rate DECREASES with training. The third option contradicts the well-established increase in capillarization and oxidative capacity.

questions.question: Immediately following an acute bout of high-volume, multi-joint resistance exercise with short rest periods, which hormonal response pattern is most expected in a young trained male?
options: Acute increases in testosterone, growth hormone, and cortisol
An acute decrease in growth hormone and cortisol with no change in testosterone
A selective acute rise in cortisol only, with testosterone and growth hormone unchanged
questions.explanation: A demanding resistance bout (large muscle mass, high volume, short rest) acutely elevates testosterone, growth hormone, and cortisol together; these transient post-exercise spikes are part of the anabolic/catabolic signaling environment. The trap second option reverses the GH and cortisol responses - both rise, they do not fall. The third option wrongly isolates cortisol; the acute response is broad, not selective.

questions.question: A parent asks whether starting their healthy 11-year-old on a properly supervised, appropriately loaded resistance-training program will stunt the child's growth. Based on current evidence, what is the most accurate response?
options: Yes, resistance training should be avoided before puberty because it compresses the growth plates and stunts height
No, properly designed and supervised resistance training does not stunt growth; epiphyseal plate injury risk is associated with improper technique or maximal/excessive loads, not appropriate training
Yes, but only if the child uses machines instead of free weights
questions.explanation: There is no credible evidence that properly designed, supervised, age-appropriate resistance training stunts growth; it is recognized as safe and beneficial for youth. The real risk to the epiphyseal (growth) plate comes from improper technique or maximal/excessive loading, not from resistance training per se. The trap first option repeats the persistent growth-stunting myth. The third option invents a free-weight prohibition that is not the issue - supervision and appropriate loading are.

questions.question: When comparing average muscular strength between men and women, which statement most accurately reflects the textbook position?
options: Men are stronger than women in both absolute terms and when strength is expressed relative to lean body mass, across all muscle groups equally
Women are stronger than men in absolute terms but weaker relative to lean body mass
On an absolute basis men are generally stronger, but when strength is expressed relative to lean body mass (especially lower body) the differences shrink markedly
questions.explanation: Men typically have greater ABSOLUTE strength largely due to greater muscle mass, but when strength is normalized to lean body mass the sex difference narrows considerably, and lower-body relative strength can be quite similar; upper-body differences tend to remain larger. The trap first option overstates the gap by claiming it persists equally relative to lean mass across all muscles - normalization reduces it. The third option is simply false on the absolute comparison.

questions.question: During an open-skill play, a point guard dribbles up the court while simultaneously tracking five defenders, two cutting teammates, and the shot clock to decide where the play goes. According to Nideffer's model, which attentional style is this player primarily using?
options: Broad-external
Broad-internal
Narrow-external
questions.explanation: Broad-external = taking in MANY cues that exist OUT in the environment (defenders, teammates, clock), which is exactly what reading a developing play requires. Broad-internal is the trap: that style is for analyzing or strategizing using many of one's OWN thoughts/plans, not scanning the live environment. Narrow-external would be locking onto a single external target (like a free-throw rim).

questions.question: A golfer stands over a putt and concentrates exclusively on a single feel cue - the smooth tempo of her own backswing - shutting out everything else. Which attentional quadrant best describes this focus?
options: Broad-internal
Narrow-internal
Narrow-external
questions.explanation: Narrow-internal = focusing on ONE internal cue (a single swing thought / kinesthetic feel of her own movement). Narrow-external is the trap: that would be fixing on one cue out in the environment, such as a spot on the green or the hole - but tempo of her own backswing is an internal kinesthetic cue, not an environmental one. Broad-internal would involve juggling many of her own thoughts at once.

questions.question: A placekicker blocks out the crowd and rush and zeroes in solely on a single spot on the goalpost as his aiming point. Which attentional style is he using?
options: Narrow-internal
Narrow-external
Broad-external
questions.explanation: Narrow-external = locking onto ONE cue that is OUT in the environment (the spot on the goalpost). The trap is narrow-internal, which would apply if he were focused on one of his own bodily/mental cues rather than an external target; the aiming spot is external. Broad-external would mean scanning many environmental cues at once, which he is deliberately avoiding.

questions.question: A powerlifter must produce a maximal, simple deadlift, while a few platforms over a gymnast attempts a complex, precise beam routine. Compared to the powerlifter, the gymnast's optimal arousal level for peak performance should be:
options: Higher, because more total muscle activation is needed
Lower, because the task is complex and requires fine motor control
Identical, because optimal arousal is the same for all athletes
questions.explanation: Per the inverted-U principle, complex tasks demanding fine motor control and coordination (beam routine) have a LOWER optimal arousal level than simple, gross-force tasks (deadlift). The trap (higher arousal) confuses 'needs precision' with 'needs more drive'; high arousal degrades fine, complex skills. 'Identical for all' ignores that optimal arousal varies by task complexity (and by individual, per IZOF).

questions.question: A 19-year-old female distance runner reports fatigue and heavy training volume. Of the following, which nutritional concern is MOST characteristically associated with female endurance athletes and warrants screening?
options: Iron deficiency, which can impair oxygen transport and endurance performance
Vitamin C toxicity from too much fruit in the diet
Excess dietary protein causing kidney damage in healthy athletes
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency is especially common in female endurance athletes (losses plus high demand) and impairs oxygen-carrying capacity, hurting endurance - the textbook flags it for screening. Vitamin C 'toxicity' from fruit is the trap: it is water-soluble and not a realistic concern here. Excess protein causing kidney damage in healthy athletes is a common myth, not an established textbook risk, and is unrelated to this presentation.

questions.question: A basketball player reports that for the first three quarters her heart was pounding and her muscles felt tense, but those physical symptoms faded once play settled in; meanwhile she kept worrying about disappointing her coach right through the final minutes. Which best characterizes her anxiety?
options: Somatic anxiety that persisted and cognitive anxiety that dissipated
Somatic anxiety that dissipated at the start of play and cognitive anxiety that persisted
Trait anxiety, which is situation-specific and short-lived
questions.explanation: Somatic (physical) anxiety - pounding heart, tense muscles - typically peaks pre-competition and dissipates once performance begins, while cognitive anxiety (worry) can persist throughout. Option A reverses the two (the classic trap). Trait anxiety is a stable personality disposition, not a short-lived, situation-specific state, so C mislabels both the type and its time course.

questions.question: An athlete tells the strength coach his main aim this season is to 'win the conference championship.' To make the goal more effective, the coach should steer him toward which type of goal?
options: A process goal he can control, such as completing his prescribed sprint mechanics drills each session
A more ambitious outcome goal, such as winning the national title
An outcome goal tied to beating a specific rival
questions.explanation: Process (and performance) goals focus on controllable actions the athlete executes, which is why they are emphasized over outcome goals. Winning a championship is an outcome goal - the LEAST controllable (depends on opponents, luck). Both B and C are traps because they are still outcome goals (just bigger or more specific); raising the stakes does not fix the core problem of low controllability.

questions.question: A young athlete who used to train enthusiastically just for the love of the sport is now paid a cash bonus by a sponsor for every win. Over the season his enjoyment and self-driven effort decline. This illustrates that:
options: Tangible extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
Extrinsic rewards always strengthen intrinsic motivation
Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are unrelated and never interact
questions.explanation: Tangible extrinsic rewards (cash per win) can shift the athlete's perceived reason for participating from internal enjoyment to the reward, undermining intrinsic motivation - the documented effect here. 'Always strengthen' is the trap: rewards perceived as controlling often reduce, not boost, intrinsic drive. 'Never interact' is false because the whole point is that the two motivation types influence each other.

questions.question: A coach wants to build a returning athlete's self-efficacy before a key competition. According to Bandura, which strategy will have the STRONGEST effect?
options: Repeatedly telling the athlete 'I know you can do it' (verbal persuasion)
Structuring training so the athlete accumulates successful past performance accomplishments
Having the athlete watch a similar teammate succeed (vicarious experience)
questions.explanation: Bandura ranks past performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) as the STRONGEST source of self-efficacy - actually succeeding builds the most durable confidence. Verbal persuasion is the classic trap: it is one of the WEAKER sources. Vicarious experience (modeling) helps but is weaker than one's own mastery, so B beats both alternatives.

questions.question: A diver's body is calm but he is consumed by worrisome, negative thoughts about failing his next dive - a clear cognitive-anxiety problem. Which psychological technique is BEST matched to this type of anxiety?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation to reduce muscular tension
Thought stopping and positive self-talk / imagery to address the worry
Deep diaphragmatic breathing to lower heart rate
questions.explanation: Cognitive anxiety (worry, negative thoughts) is best treated with cognitive techniques like thought stopping, positive self-talk, and imagery. The trap answers (progressive muscle relaxation and breathing) are SOMATIC techniques - they target physical tension and are matched to somatic anxiety, not to a mind racing with worry. Matching the intervention to the anxiety type is the key principle.

questions.question: A sport dietitian needs to estimate daily energy needs for a very lean, muscular 80 kg male athlete with about 8 kg of fat mass. Which approach does the textbook favor for this athlete, and roughly what is the first step?
options: Apply a flat 15-20 kcal per pound of body weight as the standard textbook method
Estimate resting metabolic rate with the Cunningham equation [500 + (22 x fat-free mass in kg)], then multiply by a physical activity level coefficient
Use total body weight in the Cunningham equation, ignoring body composition
questions.explanation: The textbook estimates energy needs as RMR x a physical-activity (PAL) coefficient; the Cunningham equation - 500 + (22 x fat-free mass kg) - is preferred for lean, muscular athletes because it is driven by fat-free mass. The trap is the 'flat kcal per pound' table, which is not the RMR-times-activity method the book teaches. Using total body weight (C) defeats the purpose of an FFM-based equation.

questions.question: A strength athlete already eating about 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight asks whether doubling his protein to 3.2 g/kg will add proportionally more muscle. The best evidence-based answer is:
options: Yes - muscle gain increases roughly linearly with protein intake, so more protein means more muscle
No - athlete protein needs fall in roughly the 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg range (strength athletes toward the upper end), and intakes well above that do not produce proportionally more muscle
No - because excess protein is toxic and he should drop below 1.0 g/kg
questions.explanation: The 5th edition recommends roughly 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg of protein depending on the sport and training program, with strength/power athletes typically toward the upper end (about 1.5 to 2.0 g/kg). At 1.6 g/kg he is already within the recommended range, so once needs are met more protein does not build proportionally more muscle (training stimulus and total energy/carbohydrate matter). 'More protein = more muscle' is the linear trap. Option C overcorrects with a false toxicity claim and a sub-need recommendation.

questions.question: An endurance athlete finishes a depleting two-hour session and wants to maximize muscle glycogen resynthesis. Which post-exercise carbohydrate strategy is best supported?
options: Consume high-glycemic-index carbohydrate soon after exercise
Consume low-glycemic-index carbohydrate and delay intake several hours to 'spread out' refueling
Avoid carbohydrate and rely on protein alone to rebuild glycogen
questions.explanation: High-glycemic-index carbohydrate soon after exercise speeds glycogen resynthesis by driving a rapid glucose/insulin response when muscle is most receptive. The trap (low-GI plus delay) slows refueling and wastes the window of elevated glycogen-storage capacity. Protein alone (C) cannot replace the carbohydrate that glycogen is built from, though some protein with carbohydrate can help.

questions.question: A coach insists athletes only need to drink 'when they feel thirsty' and that a couple percent of body-weight loss is harmless. Which statement most accurately corrects this?
options: Thirst is a reliable real-time gauge, so drinking only to thirst fully prevents performance loss
Thirst lags behind actual fluid deficit, and a loss of roughly 2% of body weight can already impair performance
Athletes should drink as much plain water as possible at all times to stay maximally safe
questions.explanation: Thirst lags behind the body's actual fluid deficit, and about a 2% body-weight loss can already impair performance - so waiting for thirst can leave an athlete behind. Option A is the trap that the coach is repeating (thirst as a reliable gauge). Option C is the opposite error: forcing excessive plain water can cause hyponatremia (dangerously low blood sodium), so 'as much as possible' is wrong too.

questions.question: A strength coach is hired to build a resistance-training program for a college lacrosse team. Before writing any sets or reps, what should be his FIRST step?
options: Select the core and assistance exercises that match lacrosse movements
Conduct a needs analysis evaluating the sport's demands and assessing the athletes
Assign training loads based on each athlete's predicted 1RM
questions.explanation: Per the program-design sequence, the needs analysis (evaluation of the sport plus athlete assessment) ALWAYS comes first; exercise selection, frequency, order, load/reps, volume, and rest all follow from it. Selecting exercises or assigning loads first is the classic trap of skipping the foundational analysis that should drive every later variable.

questions.question: A volleyball middle blocker wants to improve her ability to spike with more force. Which trained quality most directly maps to this demand?
options: Upper-body power and explosive strength
Aerobic capacity to sustain long rallies
Lower-body muscular endurance
questions.explanation: Spiking is a brief, explosive, anaerobic action driven by upper-body power, so training should target that quality. Aerobic capacity is the classic distractor for a power/court sport; volleyball is anaerobic and intermittent, not endurance-limited, so the aerobic option does not map to the demand.

questions.question: A sprinter has built a strong acceleration phase using resisted sled towing. Following the speed-development continuum, what is the appropriate NEXT method to develop maximum velocity?
options: Heavier sled loads that slow him by roughly 25 percent to overload force
Assisted (overspeed) sprinting, used cautiously for an advanced athlete
Continuous tempo runs at lactate threshold pace
questions.explanation: The continuum runs resisted to normal to assisted (overspeed); after resisted acceleration work, max-velocity development uses assisted/overspeed methods. The 5th ed is skeptical of overspeed (limited research, overstriding risk) and reserves it for advanced/elite athletes, which the correct option reflects. The heavy-sled option is a trap: loads causing large velocity loss (well over ~10 percent) degrade sprint mechanics; tempo runs train a different energy system entirely.

questions.question: A coach wants an interval (HIIT) session that develops maximal aerobic power. What work intensity best fits the interval method?
options: About 70 percent of VO2max sustained continuously
About 85 percent of VO2max held at a steady pace
At or above 90 percent of VO2max during the work bouts
questions.explanation: Interval/HIIT training targets intensities at or above ~90 percent of VO2max during work bouts to stress maximal aerobic power. The 85 percent option is the trap: that band corresponds to threshold/tempo (pace/tempo) work, not true interval intensity. 70 percent is long slow distance.

questions.question: A 1500 m runner needs a session that raises the velocity she can hold at her lactate threshold. Which prescription fits?
options: Tempo/pace runs performed right at lactate threshold (around maximal lactate steady state)
Repeated short sprints at or above 90 percent of VO2max
Easy continuous running near 70 percent of VO2max
questions.explanation: Pace/tempo training is performed at an intensity equal to the lactate threshold (about the maximal lactate steady state) to push that threshold velocity higher. The >=90 percent VO2max option is interval work (different aim), and easy continuous running at ~70 percent is LSD, which is below the threshold the athlete is trying to improve.

questions.question: An athlete is doing phosphagen-system intervals: maximal 8 to 10 second sprints to develop short-burst power. Which work-to-rest ratio is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Phosphagen-system training uses very short maximal efforts with long recovery, roughly a 1:12 to 1:20 work-to-rest ratio, to allow near-full ATP-PCr replenishment. The 1:3 and 1:5 ratios are glycolytic-system prescriptions; using them here would not allow adequate recovery for repeated maximal sprints.

questions.question: A powerlifter's goal this block is maximal strength. Which load, rep, and rest combination fits?
options: >=85 percent 1RM, <=6 reps, with 30 to 60 seconds rest between sets
>=85 percent 1RM, <=6 reps, with 2 to 5 minutes rest between sets
67 to 85 percent 1RM, 6 to 12 reps, with 2 to 5 minutes rest between sets
questions.explanation: Maximal strength training uses >=85 percent 1RM for <=6 reps with long, 2 to 5 minute rest periods to allow near-complete recovery between heavy sets. The first option is the trap: it pairs heavy strength loading with short (30 to 60 s) rest, which is a hypertrophy/endurance rest scheme and undercuts maximal-strength performance. The third option is a hypertrophy load/rep prescription.

questions.question: A coach prescribes a multiple-effort power exercise (e.g., power cleans for several reps) for an explosive athlete. Which loading is appropriate?
options: 75 to 85 percent 1RM for 1 to 5 reps with 2 to 5 minutes rest
67 to 85 percent 1RM for 8 to 12 reps with 60 seconds rest
<=67 percent 1RM for >=12 reps with <=30 seconds rest
questions.explanation: For multiple-effort power events, the textbook recommends about 75 to 85 percent 1RM for 1 to 5 reps with full 2 to 5 minute recovery so each rep is explosive. The second option is a hypertrophy scheme and the third is muscular-endurance loading; both use rep ranges and rest periods that would compromise power output.

questions.question: A novice is being introduced to depth jumps for the first time. Which choice reflects correct plyometric programming?
options: Start with a 40 in box because a higher drop produces a greater stretch reflex
Use a box around 12 to 24 in and ensure the athlete has an adequate lower-body strength base first
Program depth jumps on consecutive days to accelerate adaptation
questions.explanation: For a novice, depth-jump box heights start in the range of about 12 to 24 in, and the athlete should have an adequate lower-body strength base before high-intensity lower-body plyometrics. The 40 in box is the extreme-number trap: too-high boxes lengthen ground contact and the amortization phase, reducing the stretch-shortening benefit and raising injury risk. Plyometrics for the same area should not be done on consecutive days.

questions.question: During a depth jump, an athlete spends a long time on the ground absorbing the landing before jumping. Why does this reduce the training effect?
options: A prolonged amortization phase dissipates stored elastic energy and weakens the stretch-shortening cycle
Longer ground contact recruits more slow-twitch fibers, which improves power
It shifts the exercise to the concentric-only category, which is more effective
questions.explanation: The amortization (transition) phase between the eccentric and concentric phases should be SHORT; a long amortization phase lets stored elastic energy dissipate and diminishes the stretch-shortening-cycle contribution to the subsequent jump. Longer contact does not preferentially help power, and the movement remains a full SSC action, not concentric-only.

questions.question: A coach wants to develop a basketball guard's ability to plant and change direction in response to an opponent. Which best describes the quality being trained?
options: Pure linear sprint speed over 40 yards
Agility, which combines change of direction with a reactive/cognitive component
Aerobic capacity for repeated efforts
questions.explanation: Agility is defined as a rapid whole-body change of direction or velocity in response to a stimulus, so it includes both the change-of-direction mechanics and a reactive/cognitive (perceptual decision-making) component. Linear sprint speed lacks the directional-change and reactive elements, and aerobic capacity is unrelated to this specific skill.

questions.question: A coach builds a drill to transfer to a tennis player's wide defensive get: a fast, low, wide drop to the side to return a ball hit well away from the body. Which resistance-training movement pattern best transfers to this action?
options: Standing barbell biceps curl for grip and arm strength
Lateral lunge / wide low squatting pattern to train the low, wide, decelerating drop to the side
Seated calf raise for ankle strength
questions.explanation: The wide defensive get is a fast, low, wide, decelerating drop to the side, so the lateral lunge / wide squatting pattern best matches the movement. The trap is matching by body part instead of by movement pattern: a biceps curl uses the arms but not the low, wide, decelerating lower-body pattern, and a seated calf raise is non-specific to the action.

questions.question: In classic (linear) periodization, how do training volume and intensity trend as an athlete moves from the hypertrophy phase toward the peaking/competition phase?
options: Volume decreases while intensity increases
Both volume and intensity increase together
Volume increases while intensity decreases
questions.explanation: Classic linear periodization progresses hypertrophy to strength to power to peaking, with volume decreasing and intensity increasing across the phases. The trap is 'both increase together', which is not how the model works and would invite overtraining; option three reverses the correct trend.

questions.question: Which sequence of phases correctly reflects classic linear periodization for a strength/power athlete across a macrocycle?
options: Hypertrophy/endurance, then basic strength, then strength/power, then peaking
Peaking, then strength/power, then hypertrophy, then basic strength
Basic strength, then hypertrophy, then peaking, then strength/power
questions.explanation: The classic model sequences a high-volume hypertrophy/endurance phase, then a basic strength phase, then a strength/power phase, then a peaking (competition) phase. The other two scramble the order; for example, starting with peaking or placing hypertrophy after strength contradicts the high-volume-to-high-intensity logic of the model.

questions.question: A coach describes the largest division of his periodization plan, which spans the athlete's full competitive year. Which term applies?
options: Microcycle
Mesocycle
Macrocycle
questions.explanation: The macrocycle is the largest division, typically an entire training year (or up to several years), composed of mesocycles (often weeks to months) and microcycles (often about a week). Microcycle and mesocycle are smaller subdivisions, so neither describes the full-year plan.

questions.question: In a daily undulating periodization week, an athlete trains heavy strength on Monday, power on Wednesday, and hypertrophy on Friday. What distinguishes this from classic linear periodization?
options: Volume and intensity are varied within the same week rather than held to one emphasis per multi-week block
It always increases both volume and intensity every session
It eliminates the needs analysis because emphasis changes daily
questions.explanation: Undulating (nonlinear) periodization varies volume and intensity frequently, even within a single week, instead of holding one emphasis for a multi-week block as classic linear does. It does not increase both volume and intensity each session, and the needs analysis is always required regardless of periodization model.

questions.question: A team-sport athlete enters the in-season. How should the resistance-training emphasis typically shift compared with the off-season?
options: Increase volume sharply to keep building work capacity during competition
Reduce training volume and emphasize maintenance of strength/power around competition demands
Stop resistance training entirely to avoid any fatigue
questions.explanation: In-season programming generally reduces volume and shifts toward maintaining strength and power while managing competition fatigue. Sharply increasing volume in-season risks interfering with performance/recovery, and stopping resistance training entirely leads to detraining and loss of the adaptations built off-season.

questions.question: An athlete completely stops resistance training for several weeks during a layoff. Which outcome best reflects detraining?
options: Strength and power adaptations are gradually lost, with reversal of training-specific gains
Adaptations are permanent, so a few weeks off causes no measurable change
Detraining only affects aerobic capacity, never strength
questions.explanation: Detraining is the partial or complete loss of training-induced adaptations when the stimulus is removed; strength and power gains regress over time without training. Adaptations are not permanent, and detraining affects strength and power as well as aerobic qualities, so the other options are false.

questions.question: Watch a lat pulldown: the lifter sits with thighs secured, grips the bar wider than shoulder width with a pronated grip, leans the torso back slightly, and pulls. Where should the bar finish for a correct front pulldown?
options: To the upper chest near the clavicle, with a slight backward torso lean
Down to the mid or lower chest by pulling the elbows far behind the body
Behind the neck to the base of the skull
questions.explanation: In a front lat pulldown the bar is pulled to the upper chest/clavicle with a slight backward lean of the torso. Pulling to the mid/lower chest is the trap: that turns the movement into a row and changes the muscle action. The behind-the-neck variation places the shoulder in a higher-risk position and is not the recommended technique.

questions.question: An athlete performs a forward step lunge. Which observation indicates CORRECT technique rather than a fault?
options: The lead knee travels well past the toes as the athlete drops deep
The trailing knee descends to about 1 to 2 inches above the floor and does not touch down
The torso bends sharply forward over the lead thigh
questions.explanation: In a proper forward step lunge the trailing knee lowers to roughly 1 to 2 inches (3 to 5 cm) above the floor without touching, the lead knee stays over (not past) the toes, and the torso remains erect. The lead knee passing beyond the toes and a sharply flexed torso are both technique faults, not correct execution.

questions.question: A strongman athlete is performing tire flips. Which of the following is a genuine technique FAULT to correct?
options: Feet placed close to the tire in a sumo or backlift stance
Hips rising too early so the lift becomes a biceps-style curl/pull rather than a forward drive
Driving the body forward into the tire as the hips and knees extend
questions.explanation: A real tire-flip fault is letting the hips rise too high so the athlete tries to curl/lift the tire with the arms instead of driving the whole body forward into it. Feet close to the tire (sumo or backlift) is correct, and driving forward through hip and knee extension is the proper action. The bait answer (not shown here) is moving the feet far back; the close stance is actually correct.

questions.question: A video shows an athlete controlling the downward (descent) phase of a back squat at a steady tempo. During this lowering phase, how are the knee and hip extensors (quadriceps and gluteals) primarily acting?
options: Concentrically, because they are the prime movers of the squat
Eccentrically, lengthening under load to control the descent against gravity
Isometrically, because the bar is moving at a constant speed
questions.explanation: Lowering against gravity is the eccentric phase: the same muscles that extend the knees and hips (quads, glutes) lengthen under load to brake the descent, so they contract eccentrically. They act concentrically only on the way up. A constant bar speed does not make the action isometric, because the joints are still moving and the muscles are lengthening.

questions.question: In a standing barbell biceps curl, the athlete slowly lowers the bar from the top under control. Which muscle action is occurring at the elbow flexors during this lowering?
options: The elbow flexors (biceps) contract eccentrically, lengthening under load to control the descent
The triceps contract concentrically to pull the bar down
The biceps contract concentrically to lower the bar
questions.explanation: Lowering the curl is the eccentric phase of the biceps' action: the elbow flexors lengthen under load while still generating force to control the descent against gravity. The triceps are not the muscle controlling the load here (gravity lowers the bar; the biceps brake it), and a concentric biceps action would raise, not lower, the bar.

questions.question: While teaching the power clean, a coach watches the second pull. Which is a common technique FAULT to correct?
options: Aggressive triple extension of the ankles, knees, and hips
Pulling early with the arms before the lower body has finished extending
Keeping the bar close to the body throughout the pull
questions.explanation: A classic Olympic-lift fault is bending/pulling with the arms too early, before the explosive triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) is complete; the arms should stay relatively straight until the lower body finishes driving. Triple extension and keeping the bar close to the body are correct cues, not faults.

questions.question: What is the main difference in the starting position between a power clean and a hang clean?
options: The power clean starts with the bar on the floor; the hang clean starts from a standing position with the bar at roughly mid-thigh to knee level
The hang clean starts on the floor while the power clean starts from the hang
There is no difference; the names are interchangeable
questions.explanation: A power clean starts with the bar on the floor, while a hang clean begins from a hang (standing) position with the bar around mid-thigh to knee level. Option two reverses the two starts, and the lifts are not interchangeable because the starting position changes the portions of the pull that are trained.

questions.question: A coach is deciding how to safeguard athletes during lifts. Which decision reflects correct spotting practice?
options: Station a spotter to catch the bar during the catch of a power clean
Spot the barbell back squat and overhead press, but do not spot Olympic lifts
Avoid spotting the bench press because the lifter can always rack it alone
questions.explanation: Spotting is appropriate for free-weight exercises performed over the head or over the body (bench press, overhead press, back squat), but Olympic lifts should NOT be spotted because the safest response is for the lifter to drop/dump the bar. Spotting a power clean is the trap. The bench press is exactly the kind of over-the-body lift that does warrant a spotter.

questions.question: An athlete sets up for a heavy barbell bench press. Which describes the correct five-point body-contact position?
options: Head, shoulders/upper back, and buttocks on the bench, with both feet flat on the floor
Head and buttocks on the bench, with both feet pulled up onto the bench for core tension
Shoulders and buttocks on the bench, with the head lifted to watch the bar
questions.explanation: The five points of contact for the bench press are the head, the shoulders/upper back, and the buttocks all on the bench, plus both feet flat on the floor. Putting the feet on the bench removes a stable base and two contact points, and lifting the head off the bench breaks the head contact point; both are unsafe deviations.

questions.question: An experienced lifter is grinding through the hardest part (sticking point) of a near-maximal squat. What is the correct guidance on breathing?
options: Exhale fully throughout the entire ascent to keep airway pressure low
A brief Valsalva maneuver through the sticking point is acceptable for experienced lifters
Hold the breath for the entire set across all reps regardless of experience
questions.explanation: For experienced, healthy lifters the textbook permits a brief Valsalva maneuver through the most stressful sticking point to stabilize the trunk, after which breathing resumes. Forcing a full exhale through the sticking point reduces trunk stability, and holding the breath for an entire multi-rep set (or recommending Valsalva for everyone regardless of experience) is not advised due to the blood-pressure spike.

questions.question: During a heavy back squat, a coach sees the athlete's knees collapse inward as he stands up. What is this fault and the appropriate correction?
options: Knee valgus; cue the athlete to push the knees out in line with the toes
Correct depth; no change needed because deeper squats are always safer
Heel rise; cue him to come up onto the balls of the feet
questions.explanation: Knees caving inward is knee valgus, a fault corrected by cueing the athlete to drive the knees out so they track over the toes. It is not a desirable depth cue, and the described problem is medial knee collapse, not heel rise; coming onto the balls of the feet would itself be a separate fault (heels should stay flat).

questions.question: Preseason testing shows a college sprinter has well-above-average hamstring flexibility, but single-leg testing reveals his left knee extensors produce about 20 percent less force than his right. What should the offseason priority be?
options: More static stretching of both hamstrings to capitalize on his mobility
Unilateral strengthening focused on the weaker (left) leg to reduce the bilateral asymmetry
Maximal bilateral squatting only, since overall strength will even the legs out
questions.explanation: A bilateral strength asymmetry beyond roughly 10 to 15 percent is generally considered an injury-risk concern, so the priority is unilateral (single-leg) work to bring the weaker left leg up and close the gap. The excellent flexibility is a decoy - he is already mobile, so more stretching does not address the asymmetry. Bilateral-only squatting (option C) lets the stronger leg dominate and can preserve or widen the imbalance.

questions.question: A strength coach wants the preseason testing battery to be REPEATABLE so pre/post scores can be compared. Which factor most directly protects reliability?
options: Administering the entire battery on the same calendar day each session
Using a fixed, consistent test order with identical conditions, equipment, tester, and warm-up
Choosing tests that clearly measure the targeted athletic quality
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of measurement, achieved by standardizing everything, and a consistent TEST ORDER is the key piece because earlier tests fatigue later ones. 'Same calendar day' is the trap: the day of the week is irrelevant; standardized conditions and sequence are what matter. Choosing a test that measures the right quality is VALIDITY, a different property.

questions.question: A coach must sequence five tests in one session: T-test (agility), 1RM back squat, vertical jump, 1.5-mile run, and a 60-second push-up test. Which order best preserves valid results?
options: T-test, vertical jump, 1RM squat, push-up test, 1.5-mile run
1.5-mile run, 1RM squat, vertical jump, T-test, push-up test
1RM squat, vertical jump, push-up test, T-test, 1.5-mile run
questions.explanation: Correct order is non-fatiguing/agility tests first, then max power and strength, then muscular endurance, then anaerobic/aerobic capacity LAST: vertical jump (power) and T-test (agility) before the 1RM, with the exhausting 1.5-mile aerobic run dead last. Starting with the 1.5-mile run (option B) or burying agility after a 1RM and endurance work (option C) lets earlier fatigue corrupt the power/agility scores.

questions.question: An athlete completes a 12-minute run test, covering 2.75 miles while alternating jogging and walking. How should this performance be scored?
options: The pace per mile, penalized for the walking intervals
The split time at the 1.5-mile mark
The total distance covered in the 12 minutes (2.75 miles)
questions.explanation: A 12-minute run is a fixed-TIME test scored by total DISTANCE covered, and walking is permitted as long as the athlete keeps moving. The pace and 1.5-mile split distractors confuse it with a fixed-distance test (like the 1.5-mile run, scored by TIME). Distance tests score distance; time tests score time.

questions.question: A 40-year-old client has a resting heart rate of 70 bpm. Using the Karvonen heart-rate-reserve method at 60 percent intensity, what is the target training heart rate? (Use 220 minus age for HRmax.)
options: 108 bpm
136 bpm
120 bpm
questions.explanation: Karvonen: Target HR = [(HRmax - HRrest) x intensity] + HRrest. HRmax = 220 - 40 = 180; HRR = 180 - 70 = 110; 110 x 0.60 = 66; 66 + 70 (resting) = 136 bpm. The 108 trap is plain 60 percent of HRmax (180 x 0.6) with no HRR; the 120 trap forgets to add back resting HR at the end. The '+ HRrest' is the step people drop.

questions.question: A coach takes an athlete's skinfolds and uses a regression equation that returns a body-fat estimate of 12 percent. Given how skinfold-based body-fat estimates work, how should the result be reported?
options: As a range (for example about 9 to 15 percent), because the standard error of the estimate for skinfold equations is roughly plus or minus 3 to 5 percent
As exactly 12.0 percent, because calipers measure body fat directly and precisely
As a single error-free lean-body-mass number, because the prediction equation removes measurement error
questions.explanation: Skinfold prediction equations carry a standard error of the estimate of roughly plus or minus 3 to 5 percent, so the honest practice is to report a RANGE, not a single precise value. The traps treat the estimate as exact: calipers measure a fold of skin plus fat, not body fat directly, and the regression equation does not eliminate error. Reporting '12.0 percent' or a single error-free number overstates the precision of the method.

questions.question: An athlete is rehabbing a reconstructed ACL, and the clinician wants an exercise that loads the knee through a CLOSED kinetic chain (joint compression and co-contraction for stability) rather than an open chain. Which exercise best fits?
options: Seated knee (leg) extension machine
Wall squat or leg press
Seated hamstring (leg) curl machine
questions.explanation: In a closed kinetic chain the distal segment (the foot) is fixed against a surface, producing joint compression and co-contraction that stabilize the joint - a wall squat or leg press fits. The traps (seated leg extension and seated leg curl) are OPEN kinetic chain: the foot moves freely. Open-chain leg extension in particular increases anterior tibial shear on the graft, which is why closed-chain work is favored early in ACL reconditioning.

questions.question: An athlete is in the FIBROBLASTIC REPAIR (proliferation) phase of healing for a knee ligament. Which loading approach is most appropriate to lead off with?
options: Maximal isometric contractions through the painful joint range to rebuild strength fast
Submaximal isometrics first (no joint movement), then progress to isotonic and isokinetic work
No active exercise of any kind until the maturation phase begins
questions.explanation: In the fibroblastic repair phase you lead with SUBMAXIMAL isometrics because they load tissue without joint movement, then progress to isotonic and isokinetic work. Maximal isometrics are wrong this early: they spike blood pressure and, because isometric gains are joint-angle specific (about plus or minus 20 degrees), they are limited. Withholding all exercise until maturation (option C) describes the acute inflammatory phase, not fibroblastic repair.

questions.question: During a hot, humid practice an athlete collapses, is confused and disoriented, and has hot skin. What is the priority response?
options: Sit the athlete down and give oral fluids/electrolyte drink as the first action
Activate EMS and begin aggressive cooling such as cold-water immersion; do not force oral fluids
Move to shade, stretch the cramping muscles, and rehydrate orally
questions.explanation: Altered mental status (confusion) plus hot skin signals EXERTIONAL HEATSTROKE, the most severe stage of the heat-illness continuum (cramps, syncope, exhaustion, heatstroke). The priority is to activate EMS and cool aggressively (cold-water immersion). Forcing oral fluids in an obtunded athlete risks aspiration, so 'give fluids first' is the trap. Stretching/oral fluids treat the MILDER stages (cramps), not heatstroke.

questions.question: A facility serves a mixed membership of small high-school freshmen and large collegiate linemen. What is the guiding principle for selecting and arranging equipment?
options: Provide equipment that accommodates the full range of body sizes and abilities of the athletes who use it
Restrict the younger, smaller athletes to selectorized machines for safety
Limit the larger athletes to free weights since machines will not fit them
questions.explanation: Equipment must accommodate the RANGE and size of the actual athletes using the facility (adjustable loads, seat/lever ranges, varied bar and implement sizes). The two distractors are population-stereotype traps ('small/young must use machines,' 'large must use free weights'); selection is driven by fitting the athletes, not by demographic assumptions.

questions.question: A strength coach is reviewing the ventilation specs for a new weight room. Which set of values is correct?
options: Exchange room air a minimum of 2 to 4 times per hour, keep relative humidity below 80 percent
Exchange room air a minimum of 20 times per hour, keep relative humidity below 40 percent
Exchange room air a minimum of 8 to 10 times per hour (optimally 12 to 15), keep relative humidity at or below 60 percent
questions.explanation: Air should be exchanged at least 8 to 10 times per hour, optimally 12 to 15, with relative humidity not exceeding 60 percent (memory hook: '8-10 minimum, 12-15 optimal, humidity under 60'). The 2-to-4 option undershoots both the exchange rate and the humidity ceiling; the 20-times option inflates the exchange rate and over-restricts humidity. Aerobic areas need higher circulation than resistance areas.

questions.question: An athlete is injured performing a power clean while the only staff member had stepped into the office out of sight. In a resulting negligence claim, which factor is most often the decisive issue?
options: Whether the barbell met manufacturer load specifications
Whether qualified supervision (physical presence with clear line of sight) was provided
Whether the athlete had signed an informed-consent waiver
questions.explanation: Supervision is the number-one liability factor, cited in roughly 80 percent of injury court cases; constant supervision means a qualified professional is physically present with clear sightlines, and complex lifts like the power clean demand MORE supervision. Stepping out of sight is a failure to supervise, which is a breach of the duty of care (negligence = duty, breach, proximate cause, damages). Equipment specs and a waiver do not cure an absent supervisor.

questions.question: A coach is staffing supervision for three groups training simultaneously: a junior-high group, a high-school group, and a college group. Which professional-to-athlete ratios should be used?
options: Junior high 1:10, high school 1:15, college 1:20
Junior high 1:15, high school 1:20, college 1:25
Junior high 1:5, high school 1:10, college 1:15
questions.explanation: Recommended ratios climb by five with age and cap at college: junior high 1:10, high school 1:15, college 1:20. Option B shifts every value up one tier (the classic off-by-one trap), and option C shifts them all down. Younger, lower-training-age athletes need tighter ratios.

questions.question: When planning the floor layout of a resistance-training facility, which arrangement best supports safety and traffic flow?
options: Center the heavy fixed equipment in the middle of the room so it is easy to reach from all sides
Place heavy or fixed equipment along the walls and keep lifting platforms away from main walkways, preserving supervisor sightlines
Cluster the platforms by the main entrance so athletes can begin lifting immediately on arrival
questions.explanation: Heavy and fixed equipment belongs along the walls and lifting platforms should sit away from traffic lanes, with open sightlines so a supervisor can see the whole floor. Centering heavy equipment (option A) blocks flow and sightlines, and putting platforms at the entrance (option C) creates a collision and traffic hazard right where people move in and out.

questions.question: A new training facility is being sized for participants. What is the recommended minimum floor space per participant?
options: About 50 sq ft per participant
About 100 sq ft per participant
About 200 sq ft per participant
questions.explanation: The recommended minimum is about 100 square feet of floor space per participant to allow safe spacing and movement. The 50 sq ft option crowds athletes into an unsafe density, and the 200 sq ft option doubles the standard. This pairs with the supervision ratios (junior high 1:10, high school 1:15, college 1:20) when planning capacity.

questions.question: A high school weight room runs at full capacity. Which combination of records and safety documents must be maintained and readily accessible to limit liability?
options: Only the athletes' signed waivers, kept in a locked office
Equipment maintenance and inspection logs, safety data sheets (SDS) for cleaning chemicals, and incident/injury records
Only the facility's insurance certificate posted at the front desk
questions.explanation: A defensible facility keeps equipment maintenance and inspection logs, SDS for all cleaning chemicals, and incident/injury records, which document due care and support cleaning and emergency response. Relying on waivers alone (option A) or an insurance certificate alone (option C) is the trap: a waiver does not replace ongoing maintenance, chemical-safety, and incident documentation.
